### Panel Layout & Navigation (Workspace Tab)

For a **git repository**, the **Workspace** tab is split into multiple rounded panels with a 40:60 width ratio on the bottom:

- **Commits (top 50%):**Lists the recent commits in the repository. If there are uncommitted changes, a special row named- `Uncommitted changes`will be pinned to the very top.
- **Staging Area / Changed Files (bottom-left 40%):**Lists files that are modified, staged, or untracked. When- `Uncommitted changes`is selected at the top, this panel is split vertically into- `Staged`and- `Unstaged`sections. When a real commit is selected, it is split horizontally, showing the list of files modified in that commit in the top half, and full commit details (hash, author, date, refs, and message) in the bottom half.
- **Staging Details (bottom-right 60%):**Displays the unified diff of the selected file.

### Files Tab

The **Files** tab displays all tracked files in the repository as an interactive directory tree on the left, and a preview panel on the right.

- Directory nodes are prefixed with `>`when collapsed and`▼`when expanded.
- File nodes are prefixed with `📄`.
- **Expand Folder:**Select a collapsed directory and press- `>`or- `.`or- `Right-Arrow`.
- **Collapse Folder:**Select an expanded directory and press- `<`or- `,`or- `Left-Arrow`.
- **Preview Panel:**Selecting a file displays its content (up to 100 KB) on the right; selecting a directory displays a list of files and folders directly inside it.
- **File History View:**Select any file in the tree and press- `Shift+H`to open a history split-panel view, showing revisions on the left and the revision's diff on the right. Press- `Tab`/- `w`to cycle focus, and- `Esc`/- `q`to return.

### Graph Tab

The **Graph** tab renders the git log history graph / branch visualization graph.

### Branches Tab

The **Branches** tab is split vertically into left and right panels:

- **Local Branches (left):**Lists local branches in the repository, sorting the active branch to the top marked with- ``.
- **Remote Branches (right):**Lists remote tracking branches.

You can focus either branch panel by pressing `w` / `W` or using the `←` / `→` arrow keys.

### Tags Tab

The **Tags** tab lists both local tags and remote tags.

- Select a local tag and press `↵`(Enter) to checkout that tag.
- Select any tag and press `D`to delete it (asks for confirmation).
- Press `p`to push the selected tag to the remote (asks for confirmation).
- Press `P`(Shift+P) to push all tags to the remote (asks for confirmation).

### Remotes Tab

The **Remotes** tab lists configured remotes for the repository.

### Stashes Tab

The **Stashes** tab lists all available stashes in the repository with a horizontally split layout:

- **Stashes (Top-Left):**Lists all stashes. Selecting a stash automatically highlights the first file in the files list. Press- `D`to delete the selected stash, or- `a`/- `A`to apply it (both options ask for confirmation). When applying, you can toggle whether to delete the stash after applying (default is Yes).
- **Stashed Files (Bottom-Left):**Lists the files changed/saved in the selected stash.
- **Stash Diff (Right):**Shows the unified patch diff of the selected file.
- Navigate stashes or stashed files using `↑`/`k`and`↓`/`j`.

### Stashing UI

Pressing `s` / `S` inside the **Workspace** tab opens the dedicated **Stashing UI** overlay popup:

- **Left Panel:**Displays the list of all modified, staged, unstaged, untracked, and conflicted files that will be stashed. You can navigate through this list using- `↑`/- `↓`/- `k`/- `j`.
- **Right Panel:**Displays checkboxes for stashing options:- Toggle stashing untracked files with `u`.
- Toggle keeping the index with `i`.

- Toggle stashing untracked files with
- **Actions:**- Press `s`to save the stash. This opens a text prompt to input an optional stash message/name (where stashing options can also be toggled with`Ctrl+U`and`Ctrl+I`).
- Press `Esc`/`q`/`Q`to cancel and return to the Workspace view.

### Worktrees Tab

The **Worktrees** tab lists all Git worktrees linked to the repository.

- Press `a`to add a new worktree. You will be prompted to enter a base branch/commit name, followed by the destination path.
- Press `l`to toggle lock status on the selected worktree (adds/removes lock reason).
- Press `D`to remove the selected worktree. You can choose to either remove only the Git metadata or delete the folder from disk entirely.
- Press `p`to prune stale worktree metadata.
- Press `Enter`to open the selected worktree (registers it to the Home screen cards list if not present, and opens it).

### Submodules Tab

The **Submodules** tab lists all git submodules defined in the repository:

- **Name:**The submodule identifier.
- **Status:**Shows- `Clean`,- `Modified`(local changes or commit mismatch), or- `Uninitialized`.
- **Commit (Index):**The target commit SHA the superproject expects.
- **Commit (HEAD):**The actual checked-out commit SHA in the submodule directory.
- **URL:**The remote source URL of the submodule.

### Reflog Tab

The **Reflog** tab lists HEAD reflog entries for the repository, enabling easy recovery of lost commits and branches:

- **Selector:**The reflog reference index (e.g.- `HEAD@{0}`).
- **Commit OID:**Shortened commit target hash.
- **Action:**The action type (e.g.- `checkout`,- `commit`,- `rebase`,- `reset`), highlighted based on the action.
- **Message:**The action details and commit message.
- **Time / Date:**Relative age and absolute UTC date of the operation.
- **Checkout Commit:**Press- `Enter`or- `Space`on any entry to checkout that commit hash.

### Overview Overlay

Pressing `v` from any repository detail tab displays the **Overview** overlay, showing resolved paths, tracking info, and committer statistics. Press `Esc`, `q`, or `v` to return to your workspace. Press `s` inside the Overview overlay to open the Repository Settings page.

### Navigation & Interaction

You can navigate and interact with these panels in the following ways:

- **Cycle Focus:**In the Workspace, Files, Branches, Tags, Stashes, Worktrees, Submodules, and Reflog tabs, press- `w`/- `W`to cycle panel focus:- **Workspace tab:**- `Commits`→- `Staged`→- `Unstaged`→- `StagingDetails`.
- **Files tab:**- `Files`(left tree list) ↔- `FileContent`(right preview panel).
- **Branches tab:**- `Local Branches`↔- `Remote Branches`.
- **Tags tab:**- `Local Tags`↔- `Remote Tags`.
- **Stashes tab:**- `Stashes`→- `Stashed Files`→- `StagingDetails`.
- **Worktrees tab:**- `Worktrees`(main table).
- **Submodules tab:**- `Submodules`(main table).
- **Reflog tab:**- `Reflog`(main table). Focus defaults to the main panel of the tab when switching tabs (e.g.,- `Commits`on Workspace tab,- `Files`on Files tab,- `Local Branches`on Branches tab,- `Local Tags`on Tags tab,- `Stashes`on Stashes tab,- `Worktrees`on Worktrees tab,- `Submodules`on Submodules tab,- `Reflog`on Reflog tab).

- **Mouse Click to Focus/Select:**Left-click inside any panel's boundaries (including branch/tag/stash list panels, stashed files list, files list, and the files tab content preview panel) to focus it immediately.
- **Resize Split Panels:**Left-click and drag the vertical or horizontal boundary splitter lines between panels to resize them dynamically. This is supported in:- **Workspace / Inspect:**Main vertical split (commits vs details), bottom horizontal split (left list vs right diff), and left vertical split (staged vs unstaged or commit details vs files list).
- **Files:**Horizontal split (repository files tree vs file content preview).
- **Branches:**Horizontal split (local branches vs remote branches).
- **Stashes:**Horizontal split (stash lists vs diff) and left vertical split (stashes list vs stashed files).
- **Overview Overlay:**Horizontal split (overview info vs committer stats).

- **Mouse Wheel Scroll:**Use the mouse wheel to scroll vertically through the active list, commit history, branch list, files list, stashed files list, staging details diff, or files tab preview panel.
- **Navigate Lists:**Use- `↑`/- `k`and- `↓`/- `j`to select a commit, file, branch, tag, stash, stashed file, or file tree item in the active list.
- **Scroll Diff:**When the- `Staging Details`panel is focused, you can scroll the unified diff text vertically using- `↑`/- `k`and- `↓`/- `j`(line-by-line) or- `PgUp`/- `PgDn`(page-by-page).
- **Scroll File Content:**When the files tab- `FileContent`preview panel is focused, you can scroll the preview text vertically using- `↑`/- `k`and- `↓`/- `j`(line-by-line) or- `PgUp`/- `PgDn`(page-by-page).
- **Stage/Unstage Files:**Select the- `Uncommitted changes`row at the top, select a file in either the- `Staged`or- `Unstaged`list, and press- `Enter`to stage or unstage that file instantly. Press- `a`to Stage All (when focused on Unstaged) or Unstage All (when focused on Staged), which automatically shifts panel focus to the opposite list. Press- `x`to discard changes in the selected file, or- `X`to discard all changes in the repository (both ask for confirmation before performing).
- **Network Progress Bar:**Any long-running network operations (such as Fetch, Pull, or Push) will display a centering animated progress bar popup so the UI thread remains responsive and visual feedback is clear. If an operation hangs or takes too long, you can press- `Esc`to force-dismiss the progress popup and resume TUI interaction immediately.
- **Multi-Remote Selection Picker:**For write operations (pushing branch/tags, deleting tags, fetching tags), if the repository has multiple configured remotes and no upstream tracking branch is set, a selection picker popup will appear allowing you to select which remote to target using ↑↓ and Enter.
- **Manage Branches:**While on the- **Branches**tab:- Select any **local branch**(other than the currently active one) and press`Enter`to check it out (safe checkout strategy applies).
- Press `f`/`F`to fetch updates from the remote in the background.
- Select any **local branch**and press`p`to pull updates from its remote in the background (can only pull into the currently checked-out branch).
- Select any **local branch**and press`Shift+P`to push it to the remote in the background (if no upstream is configured, it will attempt to push to the first configured remote and set it as the upstream tracking branch).
- Select any **remote branch**and press`Enter`to check it out (this will switch to the branch, creating a local tracking branch if it doesn't already exist).
- Press `c`/`C`to create a new branch from the currently checked out branch (or HEAD). A popup dialog will prompt for the new branch name.
- Select any local or remote-tracking branch and press `D`to delete it. A confirmation dialog will prompt before performing the deletion. (The currently checked out branch cannot be deleted).

- Select any
- **Commit Staged Changes / Amend Last Commit:**Press- `c`from the Workspace tab or from the Inspect view to open a centered Commit popup window (active if there are staged changes OR a prior HEAD commit exists to amend).- **Compose Mode:**Type your commit message. Press- `Ctrl+C`to lock in the text and switch to confirmation state, press- `Enter`to insert a newline, or- `Esc`to cancel.
- **Confirm Mode:**Press- `Enter`to execute the commit,- `e`to return to composing/editing the message,- `a`/- `A`/- `Space`to toggle the "Amend last commit" option, or- `Esc`/- `q`to close the popup. Toggling amend to active when the buffer is empty automatically populates the text box with the message from the last commit.

For a **plain directory** the view confirms the resolved path and explains that no `.git` entry was found.

For a **missing** item the view confirms the resolved path and notes that the path does not exist or isn't accessible.

The detail snapshot is taken **once** when you press Enter — it is not refreshed while open (except for staging/unstaging actions which refresh dynamically). Close and re-open to re-read the repository state.

After every successful add / edit / delete, the status bar briefly shows `Saved` or `Deleted`. If the write fails, the status bar shows `Save failed: <reason>` instead — your in-memory list still reflects the change, but the file on disk does not.

### 🔀 Main Page Sorting

The main page repository list can be sorted dynamically using shortcuts:

- **Cycle Sort Order (**Cycles through the sorting modes:- `o`):- `Custom`(preserves your manual list order),- `Alphabetical`,- `Recent Visit`(tracks when you enter a repository's detail view), and- `Latest Changes`(based on HEAD commit timestamps or folder modification times).
- **Toggle Sort Direction (**Toggles ascending vs. descending/reversed sort direction. The top border displays the active sort mode (e.g.- `O`):- `Sort: Alphabetical (Rev)`).

## 🔧 Configuration

Gitwig stores its config in `~/.gitwig/config.toml`. The directory is created automatically on first launch.

### First-run migration

If `~/.gitwig/config.toml` doesn't exist yet, Gitwig looks for an existing config to migrate from:

- A path passed as the first CLI argument (`gitwig path/to/config.toml`).
- `./config/config.toml`relative to the current working directory.
- `./config/config.toml`relative to the executable.
- `~/.config/gitwig/config.toml`(new XDG location),- `~/.config/twig/config.toml`(legacy Twig XDG location), or- `~/.twig/config.toml`(legacy Twig home location).
- Nothing found — a default config is written to `~/.gitwig/config.toml`.

After the first run the migrated (or generated) file becomes the sole source of truth; the original is left untouched.

### Example: `config.toml`

```
 = ["Repo A", "Repo B", "Side Project", "Test Repo"]
# Event-loop poll interval in milliseconds (default: 100).
# Lower → more responsive input, higher → less CPU usage. Sane range: 16–500.
 = 100
# Sorting preferences for the main page list
 = "custom"
 = false
# Enable compatibility mode to use simple ASCII symbols
 = false
```
### Config keys

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `items` | `[String]` | `[]` | Paths shown in the main list. Managed by the in-app `a`(directory scan) /`e`/`d`shortcuts. |
| `poll_interval_ms` | `Integer` | `100` | How long (ms) the event loop waits between input checks. Lower feels snappier; higher saves CPU. |
| `max_commits` | `Integer` | `0` | Maximum commits to load in workspace view. Set to `0`for unlimited. |
| `page_size` | `Integer` | `10` | Number of lines/items scrolled by Page Up / Page Down. |
| `sort_by` | `String` | `"custom"` | Main list sorting preference ( `"custom"`,`"alphabetical"`,`"recent_visit"`,`"latest_changes"`). Managed by`o`. |
| `sort_reverse` | `Boolean` | `false` | Inverts the main list sorting direction (ascending vs. descending). Managed by `O`. |
| `theme` | `String` | `"default"` | Active theme configuration name. Managed in Settings `s`. |
| `compatibility_mode` | `Boolean` | `false` | Enable to use simple ASCII symbols instead of rich Unicode icons/emojis (prevents layout alignment issues in restricted terminals like RustRover's built-in terminal). |
| `scan.max_depth` | `Integer` | `6` | Maximum directory depth to search for git repositories during discovery. |
| `scan.start_dir` | `String` | `"$HOME"` | Starting directory for interactive repository discovery scanning. |
| `scan.excludes` | `[String]` | `[]` | Directory names excluded from discovery scanning. |
| `scan.git_only` | `Boolean` | `true` | Only scan folders that contain a .git directory. |

Gitwig writes back to whichever file it loaded from, so edits made in the UI persist across runs.

## 🎨 Font & Symbol Support

Gitwig uses rich Unicode symbols, icons, and Nerd Font glyphs (such as `●`, `○`, `✕`, `▶`, ``, etc.) to provide a premium, modern visual experience directly in the terminal.

To display these symbols correctly without layout breakage or replacement characters (e.g., question marks or empty blocks), your terminal emulator must use a font containing Nerd Font glyphs.

### Recommended Font (Bundled)

We have bundled the clean and highly popular **JetBrains Mono Nerd Font** inside this repository:

- **Location:**- `resources/fonts/JetBrainsMonoNerdFontMono-Regular.ttf`

#### 📥 How to Install the Font:

- **macOS:**Open the- `resources/fonts/`directory in Finder, double-click- `JetBrainsMonoNerdFontMono-Regular.ttf`, and click- **Install Font**.
- **Windows:**Right-click- `JetBrainsMonoNerdFontMono-Regular.ttf`and select- **Install**(or- **Install for all users**).
- **Linux:**Copy the font file to your local font directory:

#### ⚙️ How to Configure Your Terminal:

Open your terminal emulator settings (e.g. iTerm2, Alacritty, Kitty, Windows Terminal, macOS Terminal) and set the active font to **JetBrainsMono Nerd Font Mono** (or **JetBrainsMonoNF**).

### 🛠️ Compatibility Mode (No Font Install Required)

If you prefer not to install custom fonts, Gitwig includes a built-in fallback:

- Open the settings popup in the app by pressing `s`
- Focus the `Compatibility Mode`option and toggle it to`true`.
- Alternatively, add `compatibility_mode = true`in your`config.toml`.

When Compatibility Mode is active, Gitwig will automatically substitute all Nerd Font glyphs and complex emojis with standard ASCII and basic terminal symbols to ensure a clean, stable layout in any standard monospaced font.

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-pop/0.1.10/facett_pop/

## Expand description

**facett-pop** — a labelled-**progress** component. Generic over any
“N things, each `done/total`, under a phase” — bulk loads (knut-popviz’s
per-label population load), job stages, batch pipelines. A non-graph [ Facet](https://docs.rs/trait.Facet.html)
to balance the model. The consumer feeds it numbers; it draws bars + exposes
the progress as

`state_json` for headless robot-testing.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Facet](https://docs.rs/struct.FacetCaps.html)- Caps
- What a Facet can do, so hosts treat every component uniformly. All-false by default: a facet opts in to each capability it actually honors.
- [Progress](https://docs.rs/struct.ProgressItem.html)- Item
- One labelled progress row.
- [Progress](https://docs.rs/struct.ProgressView.html)- View
- A set of progress rows under a phase label.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Facet](https://docs.rs/trait.Facet.html)
- The facett **component contract**. Every facet — graph, map, pipeline, table, the ported nornir viewers — implements this, so consumers (korp, nornir, …) compose them uniformly*and*get headless robot-testing for free.

# facett_model3d - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-model3d/0.1.10/facett_model3d/

## Expand description

**facett-model3d** — a reusable 3D-model viewer [ Facet](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html). It loads a glTF/

`.glb`
mesh ([), slowly auto-rotates it (injected-clock deterministic, FC-7, exactly like](https://docs.rs/mesh/fn.load_glb.html)

`load_glb``facett-graph3d`’s `RabbitLogo3D`), and draws it through facett’s
**existing CPU painter path**— project → back-face cull → painter’s-algorithm depth sort → Lambert shade against each group’s glTF base colour. No three-d / rend3 / wgpu render pass, so it lights up identically native

**and**in the wasm demo and stays headless-snapshot-testable.

Its one domain feature is a **status tint**: a named sub-mesh (default `"eyes"`)
is shaded against a green→yellow→red ramp keyed by a `status ∈ [0,1]` scalar
(1.0 = healthy/green, 0.0 = critical/red), via
[ facett_core::render::decor::gradient_by_scalar](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/render/decor/fn.gradient_by_scalar.html). The bundled procedural skull
(

[) is the demo fixture — a status console as a spinning skull whose eyes go red as things degrade.](https://docs.rs/struct.Model3D.html#method.skull)

`Model3D::skull`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [glb](https://docs.rs/glb/index.html)
- **A tiny binary glTF (**for a- `.glb`) writer- `Mesh3d`- `gen_skull`bin to bake the procedural skull into- `assets/skull.glb`, which the component then loads back through the real- `gltf`reader (- `crate::mesh::load_glb`- **per group**, each named after the group, so the loader recovers the- `"eyes"`group by name. Little-endian; chunk-padded to 4.

- **The mesh model + glTF loader.**A- `Mesh3d`- `facett_core::rabbit::RabbitMesh`- `MeshGroup`- `"eyes"`) can be addressed and tinted independently while the rest of the model is shaded normally. The same- `(positions, normals, indices)`triple per group feeds facett’s existing CPU painter unchanged.

It builds a- `Mesh3d`- `"skull"`(cranium + jaw) and- `"eyes"`(two orbs in the sockets) — so the- `"eyes"`group is the status-tinted target.- `crate::glb`- `assets/skull.glb`, which the component then loads back through the real glTF path. # Magnus

High level Ruby bindings for Rust. Write Ruby extension gems in Rust, or call Ruby code from a Rust binary.

[Getting Started](https://docs.rs#getting-started) | [Type Conversions](https://docs.rs#type-conversions) | [Safety](https://docs.rs#safety) | [Compatibility](https://docs.rs#compatibility)

## Examples

### Defining Methods

Using Magnus, regular Rust functions can be bound to Ruby as methods with
automatic type conversion. Callers passing the wrong arguments or incompatible
types will get the same kind of `ArgumentError` or `TypeError` they are used to
seeing from Ruby's built in methods.

Defining a function (with no Ruby `self` argument):

```
```
Defining a method (with a Ruby `self` argument):

```
```
### Calling Ruby Methods

Some Ruby methods have direct counterparts in Ruby's C API and therefore in
Magnus. Ruby's `Object#frozen?` method is available as
`magnus::ReprValue::check_frozen`, or `Array#[]` becomes `magnus::RArray::aref`.

Other Ruby methods that are defined only in Ruby must be called with
`magnus::ReprValue::funcall`. All of Magnus' Ruby wrapper types implement the
`ReprValue` trait, so `funcall` can be used on all of them.

```
let s: String = value.funcall?; // 0 arguments
let x: bool = value.funcall?; // 1 argument
let i: i64 = value.funcall?; // 2 arguments, etc
```
`funcall` will convert return types, returning `Err(magnus::Error)` if the type
conversion fails or the method call raised an error. To skip type conversion
make sure the return type is `magnus::Value`.

### Wrapping Rust Types in Ruby Objects

Magnus allows you to wrap Rust structs and enums as Ruby objects, enabling seamless interaction between Rust and Ruby. This functionality is ideal for exposing Rust logic to Ruby modules.

Use one of the following approaches to expose a Rust type to Ruby:

- A convenience macro `#[magnus::wrap]`
- More customised approach by implementing the `magnus::TypedData`

Then this Rust type can be:

- Returned to Ruby as a wrapped object.
- Passed back to Rust and automatically unwrapped to a native Rust reference.

#### Basic Usage

Here’s how you can wrap a simple Rust struct and expose its methods to Ruby:

```
use ;
```
#### Handling Mutability

Because Ruby's GC manages the memory where your Rust type is stored, Magnus can't bind functions with mutable references. To allow mutable fields in wrapped Rust structs, you can use the newtype pattern with `RefCell`:

```
use RefCell;
;
```
See [ examples/mut_point.rs](https://github.com/matsadler/magnus/blob/main/examples/mut_point.rs) for the complete example.

#### Supporting Subclassing

To enable Ruby subclassing for wrapped Rust types, the type must:

- Implement the `Default`trait.
- Define an allocator.
- Define an initialiser.

```
;
```
#### Error Handling

Use `magnus::Error` to propagate errors to Ruby from Rust:

```
;
```
## Getting Started

### Writing an extension gem (calling Rust from Ruby)

Ruby extensions must be built as dynamic system libraries, this can be done by
setting the `crate-type` attribute in your `Cargo.toml`.

`Cargo.toml`

```
[]
 = ["cdylib"]
[]
 = "0.8"
```
When Ruby loads your extension it calls an 'init' function defined in your
extension. In this function you will need to define your Ruby classes and bind
Rust functions to Ruby methods. Use the `#[magnus::init]` attribute to mark
your init function so it can be correctly exposed to Ruby.

`src/lib.rs`

```
use ;
```
If you wish to package your extension as a Gem, we recommend using the
[ rb_sys gem](https://github.com/oxidize-rb/rb-sys/tree/main/gem) to build along with

`rake-compiler`. These tools will
automatically build your Rust extension as a dynamic library, and then package
it as a gem.*Note*: The newest version of rubygems does have beta support for compiling
Rust, so in the future the `rb_sys` gem won't be necessary.

`my_example_gem.gemspec`

```
spec.extensions = []
# needed until rubygems supports Rust support is out of beta
spec.add_dependency ,
# only needed when developing or packaging your gem
spec.add_development_dependency ,
```
Then, we add an `extconf.rb` file to the `ext` directory. Ruby will execute
this file during the compilation process, and it will generate a `Makefile` in
the `ext` directory. See the [ rb_sys gem](https://github.com/oxidize-rb/rb-sys/tree/main/gem) for more information.

`ext/my_example_gem/extconf.rb`

```
create_rust_makefile()
```
See the [ rust_blank](https://github.com/matsadler/magnus/tree/main/examples/rust_blank/ext/rust_blank) example for examples of

`extconf.rb` and `Rakefile`.
Running `rake compile` will place the extension at
`lib/my_example_gem/my_example_gem.so` (or `.bundle` on macOS), which you'd
load from Ruby like so:`lib/my_example_gem.rb`

```
```
For a more detailed example (including cross-compilation and more), see the
[ rb-sys example project](https://github.com/oxidize-rb/rb-sys/tree/main/examples/rust_reverse). Although the code in

`lib.rs` does not feature
magnus, but it will compile and run properly.### Embedding Ruby in Rust

To call Ruby from a Rust program, enable the `embed` feature:

`Cargo.toml`

```
[]
 = {  = "0.8",  = ["embed"] }
```
This enables linking to Ruby and gives access to the `embed` module.
`magnus::embed::init` must be called before calling Ruby and the value it
returns must not be dropped until you are done with Ruby. `init` can not be
called more than once.

`src/main.rs`

```
use eval;
```
## Type Conversions

Magnus will automatically convert between Rust and Ruby types, including
converting Ruby exceptions to Rust `Result`s and vice versa.

These conversions follow the pattern set by Ruby's core and standard libraries,
where many conversions will delegate to a `#to_<type>` method if the object is
not of the requested type, but does implement the `#to_<type>` method.

Below are tables outlining many common conversions. See the Magnus api documentation for the full list of types.

### Rust functions accepting values from Ruby

See `magnus::TryConvert` for more details.

| Rust function argument | accepted from Ruby |
|---|---|
| `i8`,`i16`,`i32`,`i64`,`isize`,`magnus::Integer` | `Integer`,`#to_int` |
| `u8`,`u16`,`u32`,`u64`,`usize` | `Integer`,`#to_int` |
| `f32`,`f64`,`magnus::Float` | `Float`,`Numeric` |
| `String`,`PathBuf`,`char`,`magnus::RString`,`bytes::Bytes`‡ | `String`,`#to_str` |
| `magnus::Symbol` | `Symbol`,`#to_sym` |
| `bool` | any object |
| `magnus::Range` | `Range` |
| `magnus::Encoding`,`magnus::RbEncoding` | `Encoding`, encoding name as a string |
| `Option<T>` | `T`or`nil` |
| `(T, U)`,`(T, U, V)`, etc | `[T, U]`,`[T, U, V]`, etc,`#to_ary` |
| `[T; N]` | `[T]`,`#to_ary` |
| `magnus::RArray` | `Array`,`#to_ary` |
| `magnus::RHash` | `Hash`,`#to_hash` |
| `std::time::SystemTime`,`magnus::Time`,`chrono::DateTime<T>`§ | `Time` |
| `magnus::Value` | any object |
| `Vec<T>`* | `[T]`,`#to_ary` |
| `HashMap<K, V>`* | `{K => V}`,`#to_hash` |
| `&T`,`typed_data::Obj<T>`where`T: TypedData`† | instance of `<T as TypedData>::class()` |

* when converting to `Vec` and `HashMap` the types of `T`/`K`,`V` must be native Rust types.

† see the `wrap` macro.

‡ when the `bytes` feature is enabled

§ when the `chrono` feature is enabled; `T` can be `Utc` or `FixedOffset`.

### Rust returning / passing values to Ruby

See `magnus::IntoValue` for more details, plus `magnus::method::ReturnValue`
and `magnus::ArgList` for some additional details.

| returned from Rust / calling Ruby from Rust | received in Ruby |
|---|---|
| `i8`,`i16`,`i32`,`i64`,`isize` | `Integer` |
| `u8`,`u16`,`u32`,`u64`,`usize` | `Integer` |
| `f32`,`f64` | `Float` |
| `String`,`&str`,`char`,`&Path`,`PathBuf` | `String` |
| `bool` | `true`/`false` |
| `()` | `nil` |
| `Range`,`RangeFrom`,`RangeTo`,`RangeInclusive` | `Range` |
| `Option<T>` | `T`or`nil` |
| `Result<T, magnus::Error>`(return only) | `T`or raises error |
| `(T, U)`,`(T, U, V)`, etc,`[T; N]`,`Vec<T>` | `Array` |
| `HashMap<K, V>` | `Hash` |
| `std::time::SystemTime` | `Time` |
| `T`,`typed_data::Obj<T>`where`T: TypedData`* | instance of `<T as TypedData>::class()` |

* see the `wrap` macro.

the [ serde_magnus](https://github.com/OneSignal/serde-magnus) crate.

## Safety

When using Magnus, in Rust code, Ruby objects must be kept on the stack. If objects are moved to the heap the Ruby GC can not reach them, and they may be garbage collected. This could lead to memory safety issues.

It is not possible to enforce this rule in Rust's type system or via the borrow checker, users of Magnus must maintain this rule manually.

An example of something that breaks this rule would be storing a Ruby object in
a Rust heap allocated data structure, such as `Vec`, `HashMap`, or `Box`. This
must be avoided at all costs.

While it would be possible to mark any functions that could expose this unsafty
as `unsafe`, that would mean that almost every interaction with Ruby would
be `unsafe`. This would leave no way to differentiate the *really* unsafe
functions that need much more care to use.

Other than this, Magnus strives to match Rust's usual safety guaranties for
users of the library. Magnus itself contains a large amount of code marked with
the `unsafe` keyword, it is impossible to interact with Ruby's C-api without
this, but users of Magnus should be able to do most things without needing to
use `unsafe`.

## Compatibility

Ruby versions 3.0, 3.1, 3.2, 3.3 and 3.4 are fully supported.

Magnus currently works with, and is still tested against, Ruby 2.7, but as this version of the language is no longer supported by the Ruby developers it is not recommended and future support in Magnus is not guaranteed.

Ruby bindings will be generated at compile time, this may require libclang to be installed.

The minimum supported Rust version is currently Rust 1.65.

Support for statically linking Ruby is provided via the lower-level [rb-sys](https://github.com/oxidize-rb/rb-sys/tree/main/crates/rb-sys)
crate, and can be enabled by adding the following to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
# * should select the same version used by Magnus
 = {  = "*",  = false,  = ["ruby-static"] }
```
Cross-compilation is supported by rb-sys [for the platforms listed here](https://github.com/oxidize-rb/rb-sys#supported-platforms).

Magnus is not tested on 32 bit systems. Efforts are made to ensure it compiles. Patches are welcome.

## Crates that work with Magnus

### rb-sys

Magnus uses [rb-sys](https://github.com/oxidize-rb/rb-sys/tree/main/crates/rb-sys) to provide the low-level bindings to Ruby. The
`rb-sys` feature enables the [ rb_sys](https://docs.rs/magnus/latest/magnus/rb_sys/index.html) module for
advanced interoperability with rb-sys, allows you to access low-level Ruby APIs
which Magnus does not expose.

`serde_magnus`

[ serde_magnus](https://github.com/OneSignal/serde-magnus) integrates

[Serde](https://github.com/serde-rs/serde)and Magnus for seamless serialisation and deserialisation of Rust to Ruby data structures and vice versa.

## Users

- `halton`
- `optify`

Please open a [pull request](https://github.com/matsadler/magnus/pulls) if
you'd like your project listed here.

## Troubleshooting

### Issues with static linking

If you encounter an error such as `symbol not found in flat namespace '_rb_ext_ractor_safe'` when embedding static Ruby, you will need to instruct
Cargo not to strip code that it thinks is dead.

In you the same directory as your `Cargo.toml` file, create a
`.cargo/config.toml` file with the following contents:

```
[]
# Without this flag, when linking static libruby, the linker removes symbols
# (such as `_rb_ext_ractor_safe`) which it thinks are dead code... but they are
# not, and they need to be included for the `embed` feature to work with static
# Ruby.
 = ["-C", "link-dead-code=on"]
```

Magnus is named after *Magnus the Red* a character from the Warhammer 40,000
universe. A sorcerer who believed he could tame the psychic energy of the Warp.
Ultimately, his hubris lead to his fall to Chaos, but let's hope using this
library turns out better for you.

# magnus - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/magnus/0.8.2/target-redirect/magnus/

## Expand description

Magnus is a library for writing Ruby extensions in Rust, or running Ruby code from Rust.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

All Ruby objects are represented by [ Value](https://docs.rs/value/struct.Value.html). To make it easier to work
with values that are instances of specific classes a number of wrapper
types are available. These wrappers and

[all implement the](https://docs.rs/value/struct.Value.html)

`Value`[trait, so share many methods.](https://docs.rs/value/trait.ReprValue.html)

`ReprValue`| Ruby Class | Magnus Type |
|---|---|
| `String` | `RString` |
| `Integer` | `Integer` |
| `Float` | `Float` |
| `Array` | `RArray` |
| `Hash` | `RHash` |
| `Symbol` | `Symbol` |
| `Class` | `RClass` |
| `Module` | `RModule` |

When writing Rust code to be called from Ruby the [ init](https://docs.rs/attr.init.html) attribute can
be used to mark your init function that Ruby will call when your library
is

`require`d.When embedding Ruby in a Rust program, see [ embed::init](https://docs.rs/embed/fn.init.html) for initialising
the Ruby VM.

The [ method](https://docs.rs/macro.method.html) macro can be used to wrap a Rust function
with automatic type conversion and error handing so it can be exposed to
Ruby. The

[trait handles conversions from Ruby to Rust, and anything implementing](https://docs.rs/try_convert/trait.TryConvert.html)

`TryConvert`[can be returned to Ruby. See the](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoValue.html)

`IntoValue`[and](https://docs.rs/module/trait.Module.html)

`Module`[traits for defining methods.](https://docs.rs/trait.Object.html)

`Object`[ Value::funcall](https://docs.rs/value/struct.Value.html#method.funcall) can be used to call Ruby methods from Rust.

See the [ wrap](https://docs.rs/attr.wrap.html) attribute macro for wrapping Rust types as Ruby objects.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

When using Magnus, in Rust code, Ruby objects must be kept on the stack. If objects are moved to the heap the Ruby GC can not reach them, and they may be garbage collected. This could lead to memory safety issues.

It is not possible to enforce this rule in Rust’s type system or via the borrow checker, users of Magnus must maintain this rule manually.

An example of something that breaks this rule would be storing a Ruby
object in a Rust heap allocated data structure, such as `Vec`, `HashMap`,
or `Box`. This must be avoided at all costs.

While it would be possible to mark any functions that could expose this
unsafty as `unsafe`, that would mean that almost every interaction with
Ruby would be `unsafe`. This would leave no way to differentiate the
*really* unsafe functions that need much more care to use.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use magnus::{function, method, prelude::*, Error, Ruby};
#[magnus::wrap(class = "Euclid::Point", free_immediately, size)]
struct Point {
    x: isize,
    y: isize,
}
impl Point {
    fn new(x: isize, y: isize) -> Self {
        Self { x, y }
    }
    fn x(&self) -> isize {
        self.x
    }
    fn y(&self) -> isize {
        self.y
    }
}
fn distance(a: &Point, b: &Point) -> f64 {
    (((b.x - a.x).pow(2) + (b.y - a.y).pow(2)) as f64).sqrt()
}
#[magnus::init]
fn init(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let module = ruby.define_module("Euclid")?;
    let class = module.define_class("Point", ruby.class_object())?;
    class.define_singleton_method("new", function!(Point::new, 2))?;
    class.define_method("x", method!(Point::x, 0))?;
    class.define_method("y", method!(Point::y, 0))?;
    module.define_module_function("distance", function!(distance, 2))?;
    Ok(())
}
```

- `rb-sys`
- `serde_magnus`

# magnus - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/index.html

## Expand description

Magnus is a library for writing Ruby extensions in Rust, or running Ruby code from Rust.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

All Ruby objects are represented by [ Value](https://docs.rs/value/struct.Value.html). To make it easier to work
with values that are instances of specific classes a number of wrapper
types are available. These wrappers and

[all implement the](https://docs.rs/value/struct.Value.html)

`Value`[trait, so share many methods.](https://docs.rs/value/trait.ReprValue.html)

`ReprValue`| Ruby Class | Magnus Type |
|---|---|
| `String` | `RString` |
| `Integer` | `Integer` |
| `Float` | `Float` |
| `Array` | `RArray` |
| `Hash` | `RHash` |
| `Symbol` | `Symbol` |
| `Class` | `RClass` |
| `Module` | `RModule` |

When writing Rust code to be called from Ruby the [ init](https://docs.rs/attr.init.html) attribute can
be used to mark your init function that Ruby will call when your library
is

`require`d.When embedding Ruby in a Rust program, see [ embed::init](https://docs.rs/embed/fn.init.html) for initialising
the Ruby VM.

The [ method](https://docs.rs/macro.method.html) macro can be used to wrap a Rust function
with automatic type conversion and error handing so it can be exposed to
Ruby. The

[trait handles conversions from Ruby to Rust, and anything implementing](https://docs.rs/try_convert/trait.TryConvert.html)

`TryConvert`[can be returned to Ruby. See the](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoValue.html)

`IntoValue`[and](https://docs.rs/module/trait.Module.html)

`Module`[traits for defining methods.](https://docs.rs/trait.Object.html)

`Object`[ Value::funcall](https://docs.rs/value/struct.Value.html#method.funcall) can be used to call Ruby methods from Rust.

See the [ wrap](https://docs.rs/attr.wrap.html) attribute macro for wrapping Rust types as Ruby objects.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

When using Magnus, in Rust code, Ruby objects must be kept on the stack. If objects are moved to the heap the Ruby GC can not reach them, and they may be garbage collected. This could lead to memory safety issues.

It is not possible to enforce this rule in Rust’s type system or via the borrow checker, users of Magnus must maintain this rule manually.

An example of something that breaks this rule would be storing a Ruby
object in a Rust heap allocated data structure, such as `Vec`, `HashMap`,
or `Box`. This must be avoided at all costs.

While it would be possible to mark any functions that could expose this
unsafty as `unsafe`, that would mean that almost every interaction with
Ruby would be `unsafe`. This would leave no way to differentiate the
*really* unsafe functions that need much more care to use.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use magnus::{function, method, prelude::*, Error, Ruby};
#[magnus::wrap(class = "Euclid::Point", free_immediately, size)]
struct Point {
    x: isize,
    y: isize,
}
impl Point {
    fn new(x: isize, y: isize) -> Self {
        Self { x, y }
    }
    fn x(&self) -> isize {
        self.x
    }
    fn y(&self) -> isize {
        self.y
    }
}
fn distance(a: &Point, b: &Point) -> f64 {
    (((b.x - a.x).pow(2) + (b.y - a.y).pow(2)) as f64).sqrt()
}
#[magnus::init]
fn init(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let module = ruby.define_module("Euclid")?;
    let class = module.define_class("Point", ruby.class_object())?;
    class.define_singleton_method("new", function!(Point::new, 2))?;
    class.define_method("x", method!(Point::x, 0))?;
    class.define_method("y", method!(Point::y, 0))?;
    module.define_module_function("distance", function!(distance, 2))?;
    Ok(())
}
```

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/src/magnus/lib.rs.html

# magnus/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! Magnus is a library for writing Ruby extensions in Rust, or running Ruby
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! code from Rust.
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//!
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! # Overview
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! All Ruby objects are represented by [`Value`]. To make it easier to work
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! with values that are instances of specific classes a number of wrapper
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! types are available. These wrappers and [`Value`] all implement the
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! [`ReprValue`] trait, so share many methods.
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! | Ruby Class | Magnus Type |
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! |------------|-------------|
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! | `String`   | [`RString`] |
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! | `Integer`  | [`Integer`] |
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! | `Float`    | [`Float`]   |
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! | `Array`    | [`RArray`]  |
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! | `Hash`     | [`RHash`]   |
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! | `Symbol`   | [`Symbol`]  |
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! | `Class`    | [`RClass`]  |
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! | `Module`   | [`RModule`] |
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! When writing Rust code to be called from Ruby the [`init`] attribute can
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! be used to mark your init function that Ruby will call when your library
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! is `require`d.
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! When embedding Ruby in a Rust program, see [`embed::init`] for initialising
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! the Ruby VM.
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! The [`method`](`macro@method`) macro can be used to wrap a Rust function
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! with automatic type conversion and error handing so it can be exposed to
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! Ruby. The [`TryConvert`] trait handles conversions from Ruby to Rust, and
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! anything implementing [`IntoValue`] can be returned to Ruby. See the
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! [`Module`] and [`Object`] traits for defining methods.
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! [`Value::funcall`] can be used to call Ruby methods from Rust.
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! See the [`wrap`] attribute macro for wrapping Rust types as Ruby objects.
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! ## Safety
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! When using Magnus, in Rust code, Ruby objects must be kept on the stack. If
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! objects are moved to the heap the Ruby GC can not reach them, and they may
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! be garbage collected. This could lead to memory safety issues.
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! It is not possible to enforce this rule in Rust's type system or via the
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! borrow checker, users of Magnus must maintain this rule manually.
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! An example of something that breaks this rule would be storing a Ruby
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! object in a Rust heap allocated data structure, such as `Vec`, `HashMap`,
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! or `Box`. This must be avoided at all costs.
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! While it would be possible to mark any functions that could expose this
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! unsafty as `unsafe`, that would mean that almost every interaction with
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! Ruby would be `unsafe`. This would leave no way to differentiate the
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! *really* unsafe functions that need much more care to use.
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! # Examples
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! ```
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! use magnus::{function, method, prelude::*, Error, Ruby};
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! #[magnus::wrap(class = "Euclid::Point", free_immediately, size)]
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! struct Point {
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!     x: isize,
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!     y: isize,
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! }
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! impl Point {
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!     fn new(x: isize, y: isize) -> Self {
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!         Self { x, y }
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!     }
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!     fn x(&self) -> isize {
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!         self.x
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!     }
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!     fn y(&self) -> isize {
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!         self.y
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!     }
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! }
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! fn distance(a: &Point, b: &Point) -> f64 {
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!     (((b.x - a.x).pow(2) + (b.y - a.y).pow(2)) as f64).sqrt()
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! }
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! #[magnus::init]
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! fn init(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!     let module = ruby.define_module("Euclid")?;
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//!     let class = module.define_class("Point", ruby.class_object())?;
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!     class.define_singleton_method("new", function!(Point::new, 2))?;
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!     class.define_method("x", method!(Point::x, 0))?;
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!     class.define_method("y", method!(Point::y, 0))?;
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//!     module.define_module_function("distance", function!(distance, 2))?;
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!     Ok(())
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! }
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! # Ruby::init(init).unwrap()
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! ```
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! # Crates that work with Magnus
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! * [`rb-sys`](https://docs.rs/rb-sys) - low level bindings to Ruby.
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! * [`serde_magnus`](https://docs.rs/serde_magnus) - Serde integration.
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//!
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! # C Function Index
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//!
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! This lists all the Ruby C API functions currently implemented, and how they
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! map to Rust functions and methods in Magnus.
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//
[109](https://docs.rs#109)// Currently unimplemented listed here, but not included in doc comments. The
[110](https://docs.rs#110)// plan is to start listing what's planned to implement, what can't/won't be
[111](https://docs.rs#111)// implemented, alternatives, etc.
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! <details>
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! <summary>Click to show</summary>
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! ## A-N
[116](https://docs.rs#116)// * `Check_Type`:
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! * `Data_Get_Struct`: See [`wrap`] and [`TypedData`].
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! * `Data_Make_Struct`: See [`wrap`] and [`TypedData`].
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! * `Data_Wrap_Struct`: See [`wrap`] and [`TypedData`].
[120](https://docs.rs#120)// * `ExportStringValue`:
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!

[1903](https://docs.rs#1903)
[1904](https://docs.rs#1904)/// Evaluate a literal string of Ruby code with the given local variables.
[1905](https://docs.rs#1905)///
[1906](https://docs.rs#1906)/// Any type that implements [`IntoValue`] can be passed to Ruby.
[1907](https://docs.rs#1907)///
[1908](https://docs.rs#1908)/// See also the [`eval`](fn@crate::eval) function.
[1909](https://docs.rs#1909)///
[1910](https://docs.rs#1910)/// # Panics
[1911](https://docs.rs#1911)///
[1912](https://docs.rs#1912)/// Panics if called from a non-Ruby thread.
[1913](https://docs.rs#1913)///
[1914](https://docs.rs#1914)/// # Examples
[1915](https://docs.rs#1915)///
[1916](https://docs.rs#1916)/// ```
[1917](https://docs.rs#1917)/// # let _cleanup = unsafe { magnus::embed::init() };
[1918](https://docs.rs#1918)/// let result: i64 = magnus::eval!("a + b", a = 1, b = 2).unwrap();
[1919](https://docs.rs#1919)/// assert_eq!(result, 3)
[1920](https://docs.rs#1920)/// ```
[1921](https://docs.rs#1921)/// ```
[1922](https://docs.rs#1922)/// # let _cleanup = unsafe { magnus::embed::init() };
[1923](https://docs.rs#1923)/// let a = 1;
[1924](https://docs.rs#1924)/// let b = 2;
[1925](https://docs.rs#1925)/// let result: i64 = magnus::eval!("a + b", a, b).unwrap();
[1926](https://docs.rs#1926)/// assert_eq!(result, 3);
[1927](https://docs.rs#1927)/// ```
[1928](https://docs.rs#1928)#[macro_export]
[1929](https://docs.rs#1929)macro_rules! eval {
[1930](https://docs.rs#1930)    ($str:literal) => {{
[1931](https://docs.rs#1931)        $crate::eval!($crate::Ruby::get().unwrap(), $str)
[1932](https://docs.rs#1932)    }};
[1933](https://docs.rs#1933)    ($str:literal, $($bindings:tt)*) => {{
[1934](https://docs.rs#1934)        $crate::eval!($crate::Ruby::get().unwrap(), $str, $($bindings)*)
[1935](https://docs.rs#1935)    }};
[1936](https://docs.rs#1936)    ($ruby:expr, $str:literal) => {{
[1937](https://docs.rs#1937)        use $crate::{r_string::IntoRString, value::ReprValue};
[1938](https://docs.rs#1938)        $ruby
[1939](https://docs.rs#1939)            .eval::<$crate::Value>("binding")
[1940](https://docs.rs#1940)            .unwrap()
[1941](https://docs.rs#1941)            .funcall("eval", ($str.into_r_string_with(&$ruby),))
[1942](https://docs.rs#1942)    }};
[1943](https://docs.rs#1943)    ($ruby:expr, $str:literal, $($bindings:tt)*) => {{
[1944](https://docs.rs#1944)        use $crate::{r_string::IntoRString, value::ReprValue};
[1945](https://docs.rs#1945)        let binding = $ruby.eval::<$crate::Value>("binding").unwrap();
[1946](https://docs.rs#1946)        $crate::bind!(binding, $($bindings)*);
[1947](https://docs.rs#1947)        binding.funcall("eval", ($str.into_r_string_with(&$ruby),))
[1948](https://docs.rs#1948)    }};
[1949](https://docs.rs#1949)}
[1950](https://docs.rs#1950)
[1951](https://docs.rs#1951)#[doc(hidden)]
[1952](https://docs.rs#1952)#[macro_export]
[1953](https://docs.rs#1953)macro_rules! bind {
[1954](https://docs.rs#1954)    ($binding:ident,) => {};
[1955](https://docs.rs#1955)    ($binding:ident, $k:ident = $v:expr) => {{
[1956](https://docs.rs#1956)        use $crate::symbol::IntoSymbol;
[1957](https://docs.rs#1957)        let _: $crate::Value = $binding.funcall(
[1958](https://docs.rs#1958)            "local_variable_set",
[1959](https://docs.rs#1959)            (stringify!($k).into_symbol_with(&$crate::Ruby::get_with($binding)), $v),
[1960](https://docs.rs#1960)        )
[1961](https://docs.rs#1961)        .unwrap();
[1962](https://docs.rs#1962)    }};
[1963](https://docs.rs#1963)    ($binding:ident, $k:ident) => {{
[1964](https://docs.rs#1964)        use $crate::symbol::IntoSymbol;
[1965](https://docs.rs#1965)        let _: $crate::Value = $binding.funcall(
[1966](https://docs.rs#1966)            "local_variable_set",
[1967](https://docs.rs#1967)            (stringify!($k).into_symbol_with(&$crate::Ruby::get_with($binding)), $k),
[1968](https://docs.rs#1968)        )
[1969](https://docs.rs#1969)        .unwrap();

[1991](https://docs.rs#1991)/// Asserts a Ruby expression evaluates to a truthy value.
[1992](https://docs.rs#1992)///
[1993](https://docs.rs#1993)/// This macro uses the Ruby
[1994](https://docs.rs#1994)/// [`power_assert`](https://github.com/ruby/power_assert) gem that is part of
[1995](https://docs.rs#1995)/// the Ruby standard library to generate detailed failure messages.
[1996](https://docs.rs#1996)///
[1997](https://docs.rs#1997)/// ``` should_panic
[1998](https://docs.rs#1998)/// # let _cleanup = unsafe { magnus::embed::init() };
[1999](https://docs.rs#1999)/// magnus::rb_assert!("1 + 2 == 4");
[2000](https://docs.rs#2000)/// ```
[2001](https://docs.rs#2001)///
[2002](https://docs.rs#2002)/// Outputs:
[2003](https://docs.rs#2003)///
[2004](https://docs.rs#2004)/// ``` plain
[2005](https://docs.rs#2005)/// thread 'main' panicked at '
[2006](https://docs.rs#2006)/// 1 + 2 == 4
[2007](https://docs.rs#2007)///   |   |
[2008](https://docs.rs#2008)///   |   false
[2009](https://docs.rs#2009)///   3', src/lib.rs:5:1
[2010](https://docs.rs#2010)/// ```
[2011](https://docs.rs#2011)///
[2012](https://docs.rs#2012)/// # Panics
[2013](https://docs.rs#2013)///
[2014](https://docs.rs#2014)/// Panics if called from a non-Ruby thread.
[2015](https://docs.rs#2015)///
[2016](https://docs.rs#2016)/// # Examples
[2017](https://docs.rs#2017)///
[2018](https://docs.rs#2018)/// ```
[2019](https://docs.rs#2019)/// # let _cleanup = unsafe { magnus::embed::init() };
[2020](https://docs.rs#2020)/// magnus::rb_assert!("1 + 2 == 3");
[2021](https://docs.rs#2021)/// ```
[2022](https://docs.rs#2022)///
[2023](https://docs.rs#2023)/// Passing [`Ruby`] to avoid the Ruby thread check:
[2024](https://docs.rs#2024)///
[2025](https://docs.rs#2025)/// ```
[2026](https://docs.rs#2026)/// # let _cleanup = unsafe { magnus::embed::init() };
[2027](https://docs.rs#2027)/// let ruby = magnus::Ruby::get().unwrap();
[2028](https://docs.rs#2028)/// magnus::rb_assert!(ruby, "1 + 2 == 3");
[2029](https://docs.rs#2029)/// ```
[2030](https://docs.rs#2030)///
[2031](https://docs.rs#2031)/// Making local variables accessible to Ruby:
[2032](https://docs.rs#2032)///
[2033](https://docs.rs#2033)/// ```
[2034](https://docs.rs#2034)/// # let _cleanup = unsafe { magnus::embed::init() };
[2035](https://docs.rs#2035)/// let a = 1;
[2036](https://docs.rs#2036)/// let b = 2;
[2037](https://docs.rs#2037)/// magnus::rb_assert!("a + b == 3", a, b);
[2038](https://docs.rs#2038)/// ```
[2039](https://docs.rs#2039)///
[2040](https://docs.rs#2040)/// Directly setting local variables:
[2041](https://docs.rs#2041)///
[2042](https://docs.rs#2042)/// ```
[2043](https://docs.rs#2043)/// # let _cleanup = unsafe { magnus::embed::init() };
[2044](https://docs.rs#2044)/// magnus::rb_assert!("a + b == 3", a = 1, b = 2);
[2045](https://docs.rs#2045)/// ```
[2046](https://docs.rs#2046)#[macro_export]
[2047](https://docs.rs#2047)macro_rules! rb_assert {
[2048](https://docs.rs#2048)    ($expr:literal) => {{
[2049](https://docs.rs#2049)        $crate::rb_assert!($crate::Ruby::get().unwrap(), $expr)
[2050](https://docs.rs#2050)    }};
[2051](https://docs.rs#2051)    ($expr:literal, $($bindings:tt)*) => {{
[2052](https://docs.rs#2052)        $crate::rb_assert!($crate::Ruby::get().unwrap(), $expr, $($bindings)*)
[2053](https://docs.rs#2053)    }};
[2054](https://docs.rs#2054)    ($ruby:expr, $expr:literal) => {{
[2055](https://docs.rs#2055)        $crate::rb_assert!($ruby, $expr,)
[2056](https://docs.rs#2056)    }};
[2057](https://docs.rs#2057)    ($ruby:expr, $expr:literal, $($bindings:tt)*) => {{
[2058](https://docs.rs#2058)        let msg: Option<String> = $crate::eval!($ruby, r#"
[2059](https://docs.rs#2059)            require "power_assert"
[2060](https://docs.rs#2060)            PowerAssert.start(__assert_exp__, source_binding: binding) do |pa|
[2061](https://docs.rs#2061)              "\n#{pa.message}" unless pa.yield
[2062](https://docs.rs#2062)            end
[2063](https://docs.rs#2063)        "#, __assert_exp__ = $expr, $($bindings)*).unwrap();
[2064](https://docs.rs#2064)        if let Some(msg) = msg {
[2065](https://docs.rs#2065)            panic!("{}", msg)
[2066](https://docs.rs#2066)        };
[2067](https://docs.rs#2067)    }};

[2336](https://docs.rs#2336)    /// Call the super method of the current method context.
[2337](https://docs.rs#2337)    ///
[2338](https://docs.rs#2338)    /// Returns `Ok(T)` if the super method exists and returns without error,
[2339](https://docs.rs#2339)    /// and the return value converts to a `T`, or returns `Err` if there is no
[2340](https://docs.rs#2340)    /// super method, the super method raises or the conversion fails.
[2341](https://docs.rs#2341)    ///
[2342](https://docs.rs#2342)    /// # Examples
[2343](https://docs.rs#2343)    ///
[2344](https://docs.rs#2344)    /// ```
[2345](https://docs.rs#2345)    /// use magnus::{function, prelude::*, rb_assert, Error, Ruby};
[2346](https://docs.rs#2346)    ///
[2347](https://docs.rs#2347)    /// fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
[2348](https://docs.rs#2348)    ///     let a = ruby.eval(
[2349](https://docs.rs#2349)    ///         r#"
[2350](https://docs.rs#2350)    ///           class A
[2351](https://docs.rs#2351)    ///             def test
[2352](https://docs.rs#2352)    ///               "Hello from A"
[2353](https://docs.rs#2353)    ///             end
[2354](https://docs.rs#2354)    ///           end
[2355](https://docs.rs#2355)    ///           A
[2356](https://docs.rs#2356)    ///         "#,
[2357](https://docs.rs#2357)    ///     )?;
[2358](https://docs.rs#2358)    ///
[2359](https://docs.rs#2359)    ///     let b = ruby.define_class("B", a)?;
[2360](https://docs.rs#2360)    ///     fn test(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<String, Error> {
[2361](https://docs.rs#2361)    ///         let s: String = ruby.call_super(())?;
[2362](https://docs.rs#2362)    ///         Ok(format!("{}, and hello from B", s))
[2363](https://docs.rs#2363)    ///     }
[2364](https://docs.rs#2364)    ///     b.define_method("test", function!(test, 0))?;
[2365](https://docs.rs#2365)    ///
[2366](https://docs.rs#2366)    ///     rb_assert!(ruby, r#"B.new.test == "Hello from A, and hello from B""#);
[2367](https://docs.rs#2367)    ///
[2368](https://docs.rs#2368)    ///     Ok(())
[2369](https://docs.rs#2369)    /// }
[2370](https://docs.rs#2370)    /// # Ruby::init(example).unwrap()
[2371](https://docs.rs#2371)    /// ```
[2372](https://docs.rs#2372)    pub fn call_super<A, T>(&self, args: A) -> Result<T, Error>
[2373](https://docs.rs#2373)    where
[2374](https://docs.rs#2374)        A: ArgList,
[2375](https://docs.rs#2375)        T: TryConvert,
[2376](https://docs.rs#2376)    {
[2377](https://docs.rs#2377)        unsafe {
[2378](https://docs.rs#2378)            let kw_splat = into_value::kw_splat(&args);
[2379](https://docs.rs#2379)            let args = args.into_arg_list_with(self);
[2380](https://docs.rs#2380)            let slice = args.as_ref();
[2381](https://docs.rs#2381)            protect(|| {
[2382](https://docs.rs#2382)                Value::new(rb_call_super_kw(
[2383](https://docs.rs#2383)                    slice.len() as c_int,
[2384](https://docs.rs#2384)                    slice.as_ptr() as *const VALUE,
[2385](https://docs.rs#2385)                    kw_splat as c_int,
[2386](https://docs.rs#2386)                ))
[2387](https://docs.rs#2387)            })
[2388](https://docs.rs#2388)            .and_then(TryConvert::try_convert)
[2389](https://docs.rs#2389)        }
[2390](https://docs.rs#2390)    }

[2415](https://docs.rs#2415)    /// Evaluate a string of Ruby code, converting the result to a `T`.
[2416](https://docs.rs#2416)    ///
[2417](https://docs.rs#2417)    /// Ruby will use the 'ASCII-8BIT' (aka binary) encoding for any Ruby
[2418](https://docs.rs#2418)    /// string literals in the passed string of Ruby code. See the
[2419](https://docs.rs#2419)    /// [`eval`](macro@crate::eval) macro for an alternative that supports
[2420](https://docs.rs#2420)    /// utf-8.
[2421](https://docs.rs#2421)    ///
[2422](https://docs.rs#2422)    /// Errors if `s` contains a null byte, the conversion fails, or on an
[2423](https://docs.rs#2423)    /// uncaught Ruby exception.
[2424](https://docs.rs#2424)    ///
[2425](https://docs.rs#2425)    /// # Examples
[2426](https://docs.rs#2426)    ///
[2427](https://docs.rs#2427)    /// ```
[2428](https://docs.rs#2428)    /// use magnus::{Error, Ruby};
[2429](https://docs.rs#2429)    ///
[2430](https://docs.rs#2430)    /// fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
[2431](https://docs.rs#2431)    ///     assert_eq!(ruby.eval::<i64>("1 + 2")?, 3);
[2432](https://docs.rs#2432)    ///
[2433](https://docs.rs#2433)    ///     Ok(())
[2434](https://docs.rs#2434)    /// }
[2435](https://docs.rs#2435)    /// # Ruby::init(example).unwrap()
[2436](https://docs.rs#2436)    /// ```
[2437](https://docs.rs#2437)    pub fn eval<T>(&self, s: &str) -> Result<T, Error>
[2438](https://docs.rs#2438)    where
[2439](https://docs.rs#2439)        T: TryConvert,
[2440](https://docs.rs#2440)    {
[2441](https://docs.rs#2441)        let mut state = 0;
[2442](https://docs.rs#2442)        // safe ffi to Ruby, captures raised errors (+ brake, throw, etc) as state
[2443](https://docs.rs#2443)        let result = unsafe {
[2444](https://docs.rs#2444)            let s = CString::new(s)
[2445](https://docs.rs#2445)                .map_err(|e| Error::new(self.exception_script_error(), e.to_string()))?;
[2446](https://docs.rs#2446)            rb_eval_string_protect(s.as_c_str().as_ptr(), &mut state as *mut _)
[2447](https://docs.rs#2447)        };
[2448](https://docs.rs#2448)
[2449](https://docs.rs#2449)        match state {
[2450](https://docs.rs#2450)            // Tag::None
[2451](https://docs.rs#2451)            0 => T::try_convert(Value::new(result)),
[2452](https://docs.rs#2452)            // Tag::Raise
[2453](https://docs.rs#2453)            6 => unsafe {
[2454](https://docs.rs#2454)                let ex = Exception::from_rb_value_unchecked(rb_errinfo());
[2455](https://docs.rs#2455)                rb_set_errinfo(self.qnil().as_rb_value());
[2456](https://docs.rs#2456)                Err(ex.into())
[2457](https://docs.rs#2457)            },
[2458](https://docs.rs#2458)            other => Err(Error::from_tag(unsafe { transmute(other) })),
[2459](https://docs.rs#2459)        }
[2460](https://docs.rs#2460)    }
[2461](https://docs.rs#2461)}

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Returns whether `self` is Ruby’s `nil` value.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use magnus::{prelude::*, Error, Ruby, Value};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    assert!(ruby.eval::<Value>("nil")?.is_nil());
    assert!(!ruby.eval::<Value>("Object.new")?.is_nil());
    assert!(!ruby.eval::<Value>("0")?.is_nil());
    assert!(!ruby.eval::<Value>("[]")?.is_nil());
    Ok(())
}
```
Checks for equality, delegating to the Ruby method `#==`.

Ruby optimises this check if `self` and `other` are the same object
or some built-in types, then calling the `#==` method will be skipped.

Returns `Err` if `#==` raises.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use magnus::{prelude::*, Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let a = ruby.ary_from_vec(vec![1, 2, 3]);
    let b = ruby.ary_from_vec(vec![1, 2, 3]);
    let c = ruby.ary_from_vec(vec![4, 5, 6]);
    let d = ruby.integer_from_i64(1);
    assert!(a.equal(a)?);
    assert!(a.equal(b)?);
    assert!(!a.equal(c)?);
    assert!(!a.equal(d)?);
    Ok(())
}
```
```
use magnus::{eval, prelude::*, Error, Ruby, Value};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let (a, b): (Value, Value) = eval!(
        ruby,
        "
          class Example
            def ==(other)
              raise
            end
          end
          [Example.new, Example.new]
        "
    )?;
    assert!(a.equal(b).is_err());
    Ok(())
}
```
Checks for equality, delegating to the Ruby method `#eql?`.

See [ Value::equal](https://docs.rs/struct.Value.html#method.equal) for the equivalent of the

`#==` method.Ruby optimises this check if `self` and `other` are the same object
for some built-in types, then calling the `#==` method will be skipped.

Returns `Err` if `#eql?` raises.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use magnus::{prelude::*, Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let a = ruby.ary_from_vec(vec![1, 2, 3]);
    let b = ruby.ary_from_vec(vec![1, 2, 3]);
    let c = ruby.ary_from_vec(vec![4, 5, 6]);
    let d = ruby.integer_from_i64(1);
    assert!(a.eql(a)?);
    assert!(a.eql(b)?);
    assert!(!a.eql(c)?);
    assert!(!a.eql(d)?);
    Ok(())
}
```
```
use magnus::{eval, prelude::*, Error, Ruby, Value};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let (a, b): (Value, Value) = eval!(
        ruby,
        "
          class Example
            def eql?(other)
              raise
            end
          end
          [Example.new, Example.new]
        "
    )?;
    assert!(a.eql(b).is_err());
    Ok(())
}
```
Returns an integer non-uniquely identifying `self`.

The return value is not stable between different Ruby processes.

Ruby guarantees the return value will be in the range of a C `long`,
this is usually equivalent to a `i64`, though will be `i32` on Windows.

Ruby built-in classes will not error, but it is possible for badly
behaving 3rd party classes (or collections such as `Array` containing
them) to error in this function.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
use magnus::{prelude::*, Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    assert!(ruby
        .str_new("test")
        .hash()?
        .equal(ruby.str_new("test").hash()?)?);
    Ok(())
}
```

    assert_eq!(ruby.eval::<Value>("[1,2,3]")?.class().inspect(), "Array");

use magnus::{prelude::*, Error, Integer, Ruby};

    assert_eq!(res.to_i64()?, 1);
    let val = ruby.str_new("1.23");
    let res: Option<Result<Integer, _>> = val.check_funcall("to_int", ());
    assert!(res.is_none());
    Ok(())
}

Call the method named `method` on `self` with `args` and `block`.

Similar to [ funcall](https://docs.rs/struct.Value.html#method.funcall), but passes

`block` as a Ruby
block to the method.See also [ block_call](https://docs.rs/struct.Value.html#method.block_call).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

```
use magnus::{prelude::*, Error, RArray, Ruby, Value};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let values = ruby.eval::<RArray>(r#"["foo", 1, :bar]"#)?;
    let block = ruby.proc_new(|_ruby, args, _block| args.first().unwrap().to_r_string());
    let _: Value = values.funcall_with_block("map!", (), block)?;
    assert_eq!(values.to_vec::<String>()?, vec!["foo", "1", "bar"]);
    Ok(())
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/value.rs.html#1405-1454)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/value.rs.html#1405-1454)

Call the method named `method` on `self` with `args` and `block`.

Similar to [ funcall](https://docs.rs/struct.Value.html#method.funcall), but passes

`block` as a Ruby
block to the method.As `block` is a function pointer, only functions and closures that do
not capture any variables are permitted. For more flexibility (at the
cost of allocating) see [ Proc::from_fn](https://docs.rs/block/struct.Proc.html#method.from_fn) and

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Value.html#method.funcall_with_block)

`funcall_with_block`The function passed as `block` will receive values yielded to the block
as a slice of [ Value](https://docs.rs/struct.Value.html)s, plus

`Some(Proc)` if the block itself was
called with a block, or `None` otherwise.The `block` function may return any `R` or `Result<R, Error>` where `R`
implements [ IntoValue](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoValue.html). Returning

`Err(Error)` will raise the error
as a Ruby exception.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-13)Examples

```
use magnus::{prelude::*, Error, RArray, Ruby, Value};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let values = ruby.eval::<RArray>(r#"["foo", 1, :bar]"#)?;
    let _: Value = values.block_call("map!", (), |_ruby, args, _block| {
        args.first().unwrap().to_r_string()
    })?;
    assert_eq!(values.to_vec::<String>()?, vec!["foo", "1", "bar"]);
    Ok(())
}
```
Check if `self` responds to the given Ruby method.

The `include_private` argument controls whether `self`’s private methods
are checked. If `false` they are not, if `true` they are.

```
use magnus::{prelude::*, Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let s = ruby.str_new("example");
    assert!(s.respond_to("to_str", false)?);
    assert!(!s.respond_to("puts", false)?);
    assert!(s.respond_to("puts", true)?);
    assert!(!s.respond_to("non_existent", false)?);
    assert!(!s.respond_to("non_existent", true)?);
    Ok(())

Convert `self` to a Rust string.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

This may return a direct view of memory owned and managed by Ruby. Ruby may modify or free the memory backing the returned str, the caller must ensure this does not happen.

This can be used safely by immediately calling
[ into_owned](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/borrow/enum.Cow.html#method.into_owned) on the return value.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-16)Examples

```
use magnus::{prelude::*, Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let value = ruby.qtrue();
    // safe as we never give Ruby a chance to free the string.
    let s = unsafe { value.to_s() }?.into_owned();
    assert_eq!(s, "true");
    Ok(())
}
```

    assert_eq!(ruby.to_symbol("foo").inspect(), ":foo");

Create a new Ruby string that shares the same backing data as `s`.

Both string objects will point at the same underlying data until one is modified, and only then will the data be duplicated. This operation is cheep, and useful for cases where you may need to modify a string, but don’t want to mutate a value passed to your function.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
use magnus::{rb_assert, Error, RString, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let s = ruby.str_new("example");
    let dup = RString::new_shared(s);
    rb_assert!(ruby, "s == dup", s, dup);
    // mutating one doesn't mutate both
    dup.cat("foo");
    rb_assert!(ruby, "s != dup", s, dup);
    Ok(())
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/r_string.rs.html#612-614)#### pub fn [new_frozen](https://docs.rs#method.new_frozen)(s: Self) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/r_string.rs.html#612-614)

#### pub fn [new_frozen](https://docs.rs#method.new_frozen)(s: Self) -> Self

Create a new Ruby string that is a frozen copy of `s`.

This can be used to get a copy of a string that is guaranteed not to be modified while you are referencing it.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-9)Examples

```
use magnus::{rb_assert, Error, RString, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let orig = ruby.str_new("example");
    let frozen = RString::new_frozen(orig);
    rb_assert!(ruby, r#"frozen == "example""#, frozen);
    // mutating original doesn't impact the frozen copy
    orig.cat("foo");
    rb_assert!(ruby, r#"frozen == "example""#, frozen);
    Ok(())
}
```
Return `self` as a slice of bytes.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

This is directly viewing memory owned and managed by Ruby. Ruby may modify or free the memory backing the returned slice, the caller must ensure this does not happen.

Ruby must not be allowed to garbage collect or modify `self` while a
reference to the slice is held.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-10)Examples

```
use magnus::{Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let s = ruby.str_new("example");
    // safe as we don't give Ruby the chance to mess with the string while
    // we hold a reference to the slice.
    unsafe { assert_eq!(s.as_slice(), [101, 120, 97, 109, 112, 108, 101]) };
    Ok(())
}
```

Returns a string omitting ‘broken’ parts of the string according to its encoding.

If `replacement` is `Some(RString)` and ‘broken’ portion will be
replaced with that string. When `replacement` is `None` an encoding
specific default will be used.

If `self` is not ‘broken’ and no replacement was made, returns
`Ok(None)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-16)Examples

```
use magnus::{Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    // 156 is invalid for utf-8
    let s = ruby.enc_str_new([156, 57, 57], ruby.utf8_encoding());
    assert_eq!(s.scrub(None)?.unwrap().to_string()?, "�99");
    assert_eq!(
        s.scrub(Some(ruby.str_new("?")))?.unwrap().to_string()?,
        "?99"
    );
    assert_eq!(s.scrub(Some(ruby.str_new("")))?.unwrap().to_string()?, "99");
    Ok(())
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/r_string.rs.html#911-918)#### pub fn [enc_coderange](https://docs.rs#method.enc_coderange)(self) -> [Coderange](https://docs.rs/encoding/enum.Coderange.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/r_string.rs.html#911-918)

#### pub fn [enc_coderange](https://docs.rs#method.enc_coderange)(self) -> [Coderange](https://docs.rs/encoding/enum.Coderange.html)

Returns the cached coderange value that describes how `self` relates to
its encoding.

See also [ enc_coderange_scan](https://docs.rs/struct.RString.html#method.enc_coderange_scan).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-17)Examples

```
use magnus::{encoding::Coderange, prelude::*, Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    // Coderange is unknown on creation.
    let s = ruby.str_new("test");
    assert_eq!(s.enc_coderange(), Coderange::Unknown);
    // Methods that operate on the string using the encoding will set the
    // coderange as a side effect.
    let _: usize = s.funcall("length", ())?;
    assert_eq!(s.enc_coderange(), Coderange::SevenBit);
    // Operations with two strings with known coderanges will set it
    // appropriately.
    let t = ruby.str_new("🦀");
    let _: usize = t.funcall("length", ())?;
    assert_eq!(t.enc_coderange(), Coderange::Valid);
    s.buf_append(t)?;
    assert_eq!(s.enc_coderange(), Coderange::Valid);
    // Operations that modify the string with an unknown coderange will
    // set the coderange back to unknown.
    s.cat([128]);
    assert_eq!(s.enc_coderange(), Coderange::Unknown);
    // Which may leave the string with a broken encoding.
    let _: usize = s.funcall("length", ())?;
    assert_eq!(s.enc_coderange(), Coderange::Broken);
    Ok(())
}
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/r_string.rs.html#1020-1023)#### pub unsafe fn [enc_coderange_set](https://docs.rs#method.enc_coderange_set)(self, cr: [Coderange](https://docs.rs/encoding/enum.Coderange.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/r_string.rs.html#1020-1023)

#### pub unsafe fn [enc_coderange_set](https://docs.rs#method.enc_coderange_set)(self, cr: [Coderange](https://docs.rs/encoding/enum.Coderange.html))

Sets `self`’s cached coderange.

Rather than using the method it is recommended to set the coderange to
`Unknown` with [ enc_coderange_clear](https://docs.rs/struct.RString.html#method.enc_coderange_clear)
and let Ruby determine the coderange lazily when needed.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-3)Safety

This must be set correctly. `SevenBit` if all codepoints are within
0..=127, `Valid` if the string is valid for its encoding, or `Broken`
if it is not. `Unknown` can be set safely with
[ enc_coderange_clear](https://docs.rs/struct.RString.html#method.enc_coderange_clear).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-20)Examples

```
use magnus::{encoding::Coderange, prelude::*, Error, RString, Ruby};
fn crabbify(ruby: &Ruby, s: RString) -> Result<(), Error> {
    if s.enc_get() != ruby.utf8_encindex() {
        return Err(Error::new(
            ruby.exception_encoding_error(),
            "expected utf-8",
        ));
    }
    let original = s.enc_coderange();
    // ::cat() will clear the coderange
    s.cat("🦀");
    // we added a multibyte char, so if we started with `SevenBit` it
    // should be upgraded to `Valid`, and if it was `Valid` it is still
    // `Valid`.
    if original == Coderange::SevenBit || original == Coderange::Valid {
        unsafe {
            s.enc_coderange_set(Coderange::Valid);
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let s = ruby.str_new("test");
    // trigger setting coderange
    let _: usize = s.funcall("length", ())?;
    crabbify(ruby, s)?;
    assert_eq!(s.enc_coderange(), Coderange::Valid);
    Ok(())
}
```

Returns a quoted version of the `self`.

This can be thought of as the opposite of `eval`. A string returned

with the exact same contents as the original.

Returns whether `self` is a frozen interned string. Interned strings
are usually string literals with the in files with the
`# frozen_string_literal: true` ‘magic comment’.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-28)Examples

```

fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let s: RString = eval!(
        ruby,
        r#"

            "example"
        "#

    assert!(s.is_interned());
    Ok(())
}
```

use magnus::{eval, Error, RString, Ruby};

    assert!(!s.is_interned());
    Ok(())
}

Mutate `self`, adding `buf` to the end.

Note: This ignore’s `self`’s encoding, and may result in `self`
containing invalid bytes for its encoding. It’s assumed this will more
often be used with ASCII-8BIT (aka BINARY) encoded strings. See
[ buf_new](https://docs.rs/struct.RString.html#method.buf_new) and

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.RString.html#method.from_slice)

`from_slice`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-31)Examples

Replace the contents and encoding of `self` with those of `other`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-32)Examples

```
use magnus::{Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let a = ruby.str_new("foo");
    let b = ruby.str_new("bar");
    a.replace(b)?;
    assert_eq!(a.to_string()?, "bar");
    Ok(())
}
```
Modify `self` to share the same backing data as `other`.

Both string objects will point at the same underlying data until one is modified, and only then will the data be duplicated.

See also [ replace](https://docs.rs/struct.RString.html#method.replace) and

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.RString.html#method.new_shared)

`new_shared`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-33)Examples

```
use magnus::{Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let a = ruby.str_new("foo");
    let b = ruby.str_new("bar");
    a.shared_replace(b)?;
    assert_eq!(a.to_string()?, "bar");
    // mutating one doesn't mutate both
    b.cat("foo");
    assert_eq!(a.to_string()?, "bar");
    Ok(())
}
```
Replace a portion of `self` with `other`.

`beg` is the offset of the portion of `self` to replace. Negative
values offset from the end of the string.
`len` is the length of the portion of `self` to replace. It does not
need to match the length of `other`, `self` will be expanded or
contracted as needed to accommodate `other`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-34)Examples

```
use magnus::{Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let s = ruby.str_new("foo");
    s.update(-1, 1, ruby.str_new("x"))?;
    assert_eq!(s.to_string()?, "fox");
    let s = ruby.str_new("splat");
    s.update(0, 3, ruby.str_new("b"))?;
    assert_eq!(s.to_string()?, "bat");
    let s = ruby.str_new("corncob");
    s.update(1, 5, ruby.str_new("ra"))?;
    assert_eq!(s.to_string()?, "crab");
    Ok(())
}
```
