# Writebarrier in magnus::typed_data - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/typed_data/trait.Writebarrier.html

`pub trait Writebarrier: `[ReprValue](https://docs.rs/value/trait.ReprValue.html) {
    // Provided methods

       where T: [Mark](https://docs.rs/gc/trait.Mark.html) { ... }
[writebarrier_unprotect](https://docs.rs#method.writebarrier_unprotect)<T, U>(&self) { ... }
}## Expand description

A trait for types that can be used with the `rb_gc_writebarrier` API.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/typed_data.rs.html#998-1003)#### fn [writebarrier](https://docs.rs#method.writebarrier)<T>(&self, young: T)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/typed_data.rs.html#998-1003)

#### fn [writebarrier](https://docs.rs#method.writebarrier)<T>(&self, young: T)

Inform Ruby that `self` contains a reference to `new`.

If you have a Rust type that contains Ruby values, and itself is
wrapped as a Ruby object, and you choose to enable the `wb_protected`
flag so that it can participate in generational GC then all operations
that add a Ruby value to your data type must call this function.

The write barrier is hard to get right. Magnus recommends you do not
enable the `wb_protected` flag, and thus you don’t need to use this function.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::cell::RefCell;
use magnus::{
    function, gc, method,
    prelude::*,
    typed_data::{Obj, Writebarrier},
    value::Opaque,
    DataTypeFunctions, Error, Ruby, TypedData, Value,
};
#[derive(TypedData)]
#[magnus(class = "MyVec", free_immediately, mark, wb_protected)]
struct MyVec {
    values: RefCell<Vec<Opaque<Value>>>,
}
impl DataTypeFunctions for MyVec {
    fn mark(&self, marker: &gc::Marker) {
        marker.mark_slice(self.values.borrow().as_slice());
    }
}
impl MyVec {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            values: RefCell::new(Vec::new()),
        }
    }
    fn push(ruby: &Ruby, rb_self: Obj<Self>, val: Value) -> Obj<Self> {
        rb_self.values.borrow_mut().push(val.into());
        rb_self.writebarrier(rb_self);
        rb_self
    }
}
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let class = ruby.define_class("MyVec", ruby.class_object())?;
    class.define_singleton_method("new", function!(MyVec::new, 0))?;
    class.define_method("push", method!(MyVec::push, 1))?;
    let _: Value = ruby.eval(
        r#"
            vec = MyVec.new
            vec.push("test")
            vec.push("example")
        "#,
    )?;
    Ok(())
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/typed_data.rs.html#1010-1012)#### fn [writebarrier_unprotect](https://docs.rs#method.writebarrier_unprotect)<T, U>(&self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/typed_data.rs.html#1010-1012)

#### fn [writebarrier_unprotect](https://docs.rs#method.writebarrier_unprotect)<T, U>(&self)

Opts `self` out of generational GC / write barrier protection.

After calling this function `self` will not participate in generational
GC and will always be scanned during a GC.
See [ RTypedData::writebarrier](https://docs.rs/struct.RTypedData.html#method.writebarrier).

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# get_kwargs in magnus::scan_args - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/scan_args/fn.get_kwargs.html

```
pub fn get_kwargs<T, Req, Opt, Splat>(
    kw:
```
[RHash](https://docs.rs/r_hash/struct.RHash.html),
    required: &[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html),
    optional: &[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[KwArgs](https://docs.rs/struct.KwArgs.html)<Req, Opt, Splat>, [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)>## Expand description

Deconstruct keyword arguments.

Extracts `required` and `optional` arguments from the given `kw` hash.

The format of the arguments required is driven by the types in the return
value. The struct [ KwArgs](https://docs.rs/struct.KwArgs.html) is returned but the types of its fields are
determined by type parameters. The type

`()` is used as a placeholder when
a set of arguments is not required.[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

This function will panic if `required` or `optional` arguments don’t match
the length of the `Req` and `Opt` type parameters.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

The rough equivalent of `def test(a:, b:, c: nil, **rest)` would be:

```
use magnus::{method, prelude::*, scan_args::get_kwargs, Error, RHash, Ruby, Value};
fn test(_rb_self: Value, kw: RHash) -> Result<Value, Error> {
    let args = get_kwargs(kw, &["a", "b"], &["c"])?;
    let (a, b): (String, usize) = args.required;
    let (c,): (Option<bool>,) = args.optional;
    let rest: RHash = args.splat;
    // ...
}
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    ruby.class_object().define_method("test", method!(test, 1))?;
    Ok(())
}
```
The rough equivalent of `def test(a: "foo")` would be:

```
use magnus::{
    method,
    prelude::*,
    scan_args::{get_kwargs, scan_args},
    Error, Ruby, Value,
};
fn test(_rb_self: Value, args: &[Value]) -> Result<Value, Error> {
    let args = scan_args::<(), (), (), (), _, ()>(args)?;
    let args = get_kwargs(args.keywords, &[], &["a"])?;
    let _: () = args.required;
    let (a,): (Option<String>,) = args.optional;
    let _: () = args.splat;
    let a = a.unwrap_or_else(|| String::from("foo"));
    // ...
}
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    ruby.class_object()
        .define_method("test", method!(test, -1))?;
    Ok(())
}
```
or, specifying the types slightly differently:

```
use magnus::{
    method,
    prelude::*,
    scan_args::{get_kwargs, scan_args},
    Error, RHash, Ruby, Value,
};
fn test(_rb_self: Value, args: &[Value]) -> Result<Value, Error> {
    let args = scan_args::<(), (), (), (), RHash, ()>(args)?;
    let args = get_kwargs::<_, (), (Option<String>,), ()>(args.keywords, &[], &["a"])?;
    let (a,) = args.optional;
    let a = a.unwrap_or_else(|| String::from("foo"));
    // ...
}
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    ruby.class_object()
        .define_method("test", method!(test, -1))?;

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/numeric.rs.html#209-224)#### fn [coerce_bit](https://docs.rs#method.coerce_bit)<T, ID, U>(self, other: T, op: ID) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<U, [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)>

#### fn [coerce_bit](https://docs.rs#method.coerce_bit)<T, ID, U>(self, other: T, op: ID) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<U, [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)>

Apply the operator `op` with coercion.

As Ruby’s operators are implemented as methods, this function can be
thought of as a specialised version of [ Value::funcall](https://docs.rs/value/struct.Value.html#method.funcall), just for
subclasses of

`Numeric`, and that follows Ruby’s coercion protocol.Returns `Ok(U)` if the method returns without error and the return
value converts to a `U`, or returns Err if the method raises or the
conversion fails.

The returned errors are tailored for bitwise operators such as `|`,
`^`, etc.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
use magnus::{Error, Numeric, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let a = ruby.integer_from_i64(0b00000011);
    let b = ruby.integer_from_i64(0b00001110);
    let result: i64 = a.coerce_cmp(b, "^")?;
    assert_eq!(result, 0b00001101);
    Ok(())
}
```

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# protect in magnus::rb_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/rb_sys/fn.protect.html

**crate feature**only.

`rb-sys`## Expand description

Calls the given closure, catching all cases of unwinding from Ruby
returning them as an [ Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html).

The most common will be exceptions, but this will also catch `throw`,
`break`, `next`, `return` from a block, etc.

All functions exposed by Magnus that call Ruby in a way that may unwind
already use this internally, this should only be required to wrap functions
from [rb-sys](https://docs.rs/rb-sys/0.9.128/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rb_sys/index.html).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/r_match.rs.html#89-92)#### pub fn [nth_defined](https://docs.rs#method.nth_defined)(self, n: [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.isize.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/r_match.rs.html#89-92)

#### pub fn [nth_defined](https://docs.rs#method.nth_defined)(self, n: [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.isize.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)>

Returns whether the `n`th capture group is set.

Returns `Some(true)` when there is an `n`th capture and it has a value.
Returns `Some(false)` when there is an `n`th capture but it is empty.
Returns `None` when there is no `n`th capture.

This function is similar to [ nth_match](https://docs.rs/struct.RMatch.html#method.nth_match), but can be
used to avoid allocating a Ruby string if the value of the capture is
not needed.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use magnus::{Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let regexp = ruby.reg_new(".([a-z])([a-z]*)([0-9])?", Default::default())?;
    regexp.reg_match("ex")?;
    let match_data = ruby.backref_get().unwrap();
    // 0th group is the whole match
    assert_eq!(match_data.nth_defined(0), Some(true));
    // the `([a-z])` group
    assert_eq!(match_data.nth_defined(1), Some(true));
    // the `([a-z]*)` group
    assert_eq!(match_data.nth_defined(2), Some(true));
    // the `([0-9])?` group
    assert_eq!(match_data.nth_defined(3), Some(false));
    // no 4th group
    assert_eq!(match_data.nth_defined(4), None);
    Ok(())
}
```
Returns the string captured by the `n`th capture group.

Returns `None` when there is no `n`th capture.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use magnus::{Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let regexp = ruby.reg_new(".([a-z])([a-z]*)([0-9])?", Default::default())?;
    regexp.reg_match("ex")?;
    let match_data = ruby.backref_get().unwrap();
    // 0th group is the whole match
    assert_eq!(
        match_data.nth_match(0).map(|s| s.to_string().unwrap()),
        Some(String::from("ex"))
    );
    // the `([a-z])` group
    assert_eq!(
        match_data.nth_match(1).map(|s| s.to_string().unwrap()),
        Some(String::from("x"))
    );
    // the `([a-z]*)` group
    assert_eq!(
        match_data.nth_match(2).map(|s| s.to_string().unwrap()),
        Some(String::from(""))
    );
    // the `([0-9])?` group
    assert_eq!(
        match_data.nth_match(3).map(|s| s.to_string().unwrap()),
        None
    );
    // no 4th group
    assert_eq!(
        match_data.nth_match(4).map(|s| s.to_string().unwrap()),
        None
    );
    Ok(())
}
```

# scan_args in magnus::scan_args - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/scan_args/fn.scan_args.html

```
pub fn scan_args<Req, Opt, Splat, Trail, Kw, Block>(
    args: &[
```
[Value](https://docs.rs/value/struct.Value.html)],
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Args](https://docs.rs/struct.Args.html)<Req, Opt, Splat, Trail, Kw, Block>, [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)>## Expand description

Retrieves arguments from a slice.

This function can be used to implement Ruby methods with more complex signatures, including optional arguments and ‘splats’.

The format of the arguments required is driven by the types in the return
value. The struct [ Args](https://docs.rs/struct.Args.html) is returned but the types of its fields are
determined by type parameters. The type

`()` is used as a placeholder when
a set of arguments is not required.[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

`TCPServer::new`’s argument handling. This is roughly equivalent to
`def new(hostname=nil, port)`.

```
use magnus::{function, prelude::*, scan_args::scan_args, Error, Ruby, Value};
fn tcp_svr_init(args: &[Value]) -> Result<Value, Error> {
    let args = scan_args(args)?;
    let _: () = args.required;
    let (hostname,): (Option<String>,) = args.optional;
    let _: () = args.splat;
    let (port,): (u16,) = args.trailing;
    let _: () = args.keywords;
    let _: () = args.block;
    // ...
}
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let class = ruby.define_class("TCPServer", ruby.class_object())?;
    class.define_singleton_method("new", function!(tcp_svr_init, -1))?;
    Ok(())
}
```
The same example as above, specifying the types slightly differently.

```
use magnus::{function, prelude::*, scan_args::scan_args, Error, Ruby, Value};
fn tcp_svr_init(args: &[Value]) -> Result<Value, Error> {
    let args = scan_args::<(), (Option<String>,), (), (u16,), (), ()>(args)?;
    let (hostname,) = args.optional;
    let (port,) = args.trailing;
    // ...
}
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let class = ruby.define_class("TCPServer", ruby.class_object())?;
    class.define_singleton_method("new", function!(tcp_svr_init, -1))?;
    Ok(())
}
```
`Addrinfo::getaddrinfo`’s argument handling. This is roughly equivalent to
`def getaddrinfo(nodename, service, family=nil, socktype=nil, protocol=nil, flags=nil, timeout: nil)`:

```
use magnus::{function, prelude::*, scan_args::{get_kwargs, scan_args}, Error, Ruby, Symbol, Value};
fn getaddrinfo(args: &[Value]) -> Result<Value, Error> {
    let args = scan_args::<_, _, (), (), _, ()>(args)?;
    let (nodename, service): (String, u16) = args.required;
    let (family, socktype, protocol, flags): (
        Option<Symbol>,
        Option<Symbol>,
        Option<i64>,
        Option<i64>,
    ) = args.optional;
    let kw = get_kwargs::<_, (), (Option<usize>,), ()>(args.keywords, &[], &["timeout"])?;
    let (timeout,) = kw.optional;
    // ...
}
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let class = ruby.define_class("Addrinfo", ruby.class_object())?;
    class.define_singleton_method("getaddrinfo", function!(getaddrinfo, -1))?;
    Ok(())
}

use magnus::{prelude::*, rb_assert, Error, RStruct, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let struct_class = ruby.define_struct(None, ("foo", "bar", "baz"))?;
    let instance = RStruct::from_value(struct_class.new_instance((1, 2, 3))?).unwrap();
    instance.aset(0, 4)?;
    rb_assert!("instance.foo == 4", instance);
    instance.aset("bar", 5)?;
    rb_assert!("instance.bar == 5", instance);
    instance.aset(ruby.to_symbol("baz"), 6)?;
    rb_assert!("instance.baz == 6", instance);
    Ok(())
}
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/thread.rs.html#532-543)#### pub fn [local_aref](https://docs.rs#method.local_aref)<I, T>(self, key: I) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/thread.rs.html#532-543)

#### pub fn [local_aref](https://docs.rs#method.local_aref)<I, T>(self, key: I) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)>

Get the value for `key` from the Fiber-local storage of the Fiber
currently executing on the thread `self`.

When Fibers were added to Ruby this method became Fiber-local. If only a single Fiber is run on a thread then this acts exactly like thread-local storage. Ruby’s C API does not expose true thread local storage.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use magnus::{Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let current = ruby.thread_current();
    let val: Option<String> = current.local_aref("example")?;
    assert!(val.is_none());
    let other = ruby.thread_create(|ruby| {
        ruby.thread_stop()?;
        let val: String = ruby.thread_current().local_aref("example")?;
        assert_eq!(val, "test");
        Ok(())
    });
    current.local_aset("example", "foo")?;
    other.local_aset("example", "test")?;
    let val: String = current.local_aref("example")?;
    assert_eq!(val, "foo");
    other.run()?;
    Ok(())
}
```

```
use magnus::{eval, kwargs, prelude::*, Error, RClass, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let cls: RClass = eval!(
        ruby,
        r#"
            class Foo
              def initialize(bar, baz:)
                @bar = bar
                @baz = baz
              end
              attr_reader(:bar, :baz)
            end
            Object.const_get(:Foo)
        "#
    )?;
    let instance = cls.new_instance((1, kwargs!("baz" => 2)))?;
    assert!(instance.is_kind_of(cls));
    let bar: i32 = instance.funcall("bar", ())?;
    assert_eq!(bar, 1);
    let baz: i32 = instance.funcall("baz", ())?;
    assert_eq!(baz, 2);
    Ok(())
}
```

    assert!(klass.equal(ruby.class_object())?);
    Ok(())
}
```
Return the name of `self`.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Ruby may modify or free the memory backing the returned str, the caller must ensure this does not happen.

This can be used safely by immediately calling
[ into_owned](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/borrow/enum.Cow.html#method.into_owned) on the return value.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
use magnus::{prelude::*, Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let value = ruby.class_hash();
    // safe as we never give Ruby a chance to free the string.
    let s = unsafe { value.name() }.into_owned();
    assert_eq!(s, "Hash");
    Ok(())
}
```
```
use magnus::{prelude::*, Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let value = ruby.exception_standard_error();
    // safe as we never give Ruby a chance to free the string.
    let s = unsafe { value.name() }.into_owned();
    assert_eq!(s, "StandardError");
    Ok(())
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/class.rs.html#444-467)#### fn [define_alloc_func](https://docs.rs#method.define_alloc_func)<T>(self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/class.rs.html#444-467)

#### fn [define_alloc_func](https://docs.rs#method.define_alloc_func)<T>(self)

Define an allocator function for `self` using `T`’s [ Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html)
implementation.

In Ruby creating a new object has two steps, first the object is
allocated, and then it is initialised. Allocating the object is handled
by the `new` class method, which then also calls `initialize` on the
newly allocated object.

This does not map well to Rust, where data is allocated and initialised
in a single step. For this reason most examples in this documentation
show defining the `new` class method directly, opting out of the two
step allocate and then initialise process. However, this means the
class can’t be subclassed in Ruby.

Defining an allocator function allows a class be subclassed with the
normal Ruby behaviour of calling the `initialize` method.

Be aware when creating an instance of once of a class with an allocator
function from Rust it must be done with [ Class::new_instance](https://docs.rs/trait.Class.html#tymethod.new_instance) to call
the allocator and then the

`initialize` method.[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if `self` and `<T as TypedData>::class()` are not the same class.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples

```
use std::cell::RefCell;
use magnus::{function, method, prelude::*, wrap, Error, RClass, Ruby, Value};
#[derive(Default)]
struct Point {
    x: isize,
    y: isize,
}
#[derive(Default)]
#[wrap(class = "Point")]
struct MutPoint(RefCell<Point>);
impl MutPoint {
    fn initialize(&self, x: isize, y: isize) {
        let mut this = self.0.borrow_mut();
        this.x = x;
        this.y = y;
    }
    // bypasses initialize
    fn create(x: isize, y: isize) -> MutPoint {
        MutPoint(RefCell::new(Point { x, y }))
    }
    // calls initialize
    fn call_new(class: RClass, x: isize, y: isize) -> Result<Value, Error> {
        class.new_instance((x, y))
    }
    fn distance(&self, other: &MutPoint) -> f64 {
        let a = self.0.borrow();
        let b = other.0.borrow();
        (((b.x - a.x).pow(2) + (b.y - a.y).pow(2)) as f64).sqrt()
    }
}
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let class = ruby.define_class("Point", ruby.class_object())?;
    class.define_alloc_func::<MutPoint>();
    class.define_singleton_method("create", function!(MutPoint::create, 2))?;
    class.define_singleton_method("call_new", method!(MutPoint::call_new, 2))?;
    class.define_method("initialize", method!(MutPoint::initialize, 2))?;
    class.define_method("distance", method!(MutPoint::distance, 1))?;
    let d: f64 = ruby.eval(
        "
          class OffsetPoint < Point
            def initialize(offset, x, y)
              super(x + offset, y + offset)
            end
          end
          a = Point.new(1, 1)
          b = OffsetPoint.new(2, 3, 3)
          a.distance(b).round(2)
        ",
    )?;
    assert_eq!(d, 5.66);
    Ok(())
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/class.rs.html#497-515)#### fn [undef_default_alloc_func](https://docs.rs#method.undef_default_alloc_func)(self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/class.rs.html#497-515)

#### fn [undef_default_alloc_func](https://docs.rs#method.undef_default_alloc_func)(self)

Remove the allocator function of a class if it is Ruby’s default allocator function.

Useful for RTypedData, where instances should not be allocated by
the default allocate function. `#[derive(TypedData)]` and `#[wrap]`
take care of undefining the allocator function, you do not need
to use `undef_default_alloc_func` if you’re using one of those.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

```
use magnus::{Class, Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let class = ruby.define_class("Point", ruby.class_object())?;
    class.undef_default_alloc_func();
    let instance = class.new_instance(());
    assert_eq!(
        "allocator undefined for Point",
        instance.err().unwrap().to_string()
    );
    Ok(())
}
```

# Yield in magnus::block - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/block/enum.Yield.html

```
pub enum Yield<I> {
    Iter(I),
    Enumerator(
```
[Enumerator](https://docs.rs/struct.Enumerator.html)),
}## Expand description

Helper type for functions that either yield a single value to a block or return an Enumerator.

`I` must implement `Iterator<Item = T>`, where `T` implements [ IntoValue](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoValue.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use magnus::{block::Yield, method, prelude::*, rb_assert, Error, Ruby, Value};
fn count_to_3(ruby: &Ruby, rb_self: Value) -> Yield<impl Iterator<Item = u8>> {
    if ruby.block_given() {
        Yield::Iter(1..=3)
    } else {
        Yield::Enumerator(rb_self.enumeratorize("count_to_3", ()))
    }
}
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    ruby.define_global_function("count_to_3", method!(count_to_3, 0));
    // call Ruby method with a block.
    let a = ruby.ary_new();
    rb_assert!(ruby, "count_to_3 {|i| a << i} == nil", a);
    rb_assert!(ruby, "a == [1, 2, 3]", a);
    // call Ruby method without a block.
    let enumerator: Value = ruby.eval("count_to_3").unwrap();
    rb_assert!(ruby, "enumerator.next == 1", enumerator);
    rb_assert!(ruby, "enumerator.next == 2", enumerator);
    Ok(())
}
```

# Cleanup in magnus::embed - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/embed/struct.Cleanup.html

`pub struct Cleanup(/* private fields */);`**crate feature**only.

`embed`## Expand description

Create a new `Proc`.

As `block` is a function pointer, only functions and closures that do
not capture any variables are permitted. For more flexibility (at the
cost of allocating) see [ proc_from_fn](https://docs.rs/struct.Ruby.html#method.proc_from_fn).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use magnus::{prelude::*, rb_assert, Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let proc = ruby.proc_new(|_ruby, args, _block| {
        let acc = i64::try_convert(*args.get(0).unwrap())?;
        let i = i64::try_convert(*args.get(1).unwrap())?;
        Ok(acc + i)
    });
    rb_assert!(ruby, "proc.call(1, 2) == 3", proc);
    rb_assert!(ruby, "[1, 2, 3, 4, 5].inject(&proc) == 15", proc);
    Ok(())
}
```

Create a new `Proc`.

See also [ proc_new](https://docs.rs/struct.Ruby.html#method.proc_new), which is more efficient when

```
use magnus::{prelude::*, rb_assert, Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut count = 0;
    let proc = ruby.proc_from_fn(move |_ruby, args, _block| {
        let step = i64::try_convert(*args.get(0).unwrap())?;
        count += step;
        Ok(count)
    });
    rb_assert!(ruby, "proc.call(1) == 1", proc);
    rb_assert!(ruby, "proc.call(1) == 2", proc);
    rb_assert!(ruby, "proc.call(2) == 4", proc);
    Ok(())
}

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/error.rs.html#72-84)#### pub fn [iter_break_value](https://docs.rs#method.iter_break_value)<T>(&self, val: T) -> [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/error.rs.html#72-84)

#### pub fn [iter_break_value](https://docs.rs#method.iter_break_value)<T>(&self, val: T) -> [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)

Create a new error that will break from a loop when returned to Ruby.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-47)Examples

```
use magnus::{prelude::*, Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let i: i64 =
        ruby.range_new(1, 100, false)?
            .block_call("each", (), |ruby, args, _block| {
                let i = i64::try_convert(*args.get(0).unwrap())?;
                if i % 3 == 0 && i % 5 == 0 {
                    Err(ruby.iter_break_value(i))
                } else {
                    Ok(())
                }
            })?;
    assert_eq!(i, 15);
    Ok(())
}
```
Outputs `s` to Ruby’s stderr if Ruby is configured to output warnings.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/fiber.rs.html#76-113)`ruby_gte_3_1`

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/fiber.rs.html#76-113)

**only.**

`ruby_gte_3_1`Create a Ruby Fiber.

As `func` is a function pointer, only functions and closures that do
not capture any variables are permitted. For more flexibility (at the
cost of allocating) see [ fiber_new_from_fn](https://docs.rs/struct.Ruby.html#method.fiber_new_from_fn).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-84)Examples

```
use magnus::{prelude::*, rb_assert, Error, Ruby, Value};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let fib = ruby.fiber_new(Default::default(), |ruby, args, _block| {
        let mut a = u64::try_convert(*args.get(0).unwrap())?;
        let mut b = u64::try_convert(*args.get(1).unwrap())?;
        while let Some(c) = a.checked_add(b) {
            let _: Value = ruby.fiber_yield((c,))?;
            a = b;
            b = c;
        }
        Ok(())
    })?;
    rb_assert!(ruby, "fib.resume(0, 1) == 1", fib);
    rb_assert!(ruby, "fib.resume == 2", fib);
    rb_assert!(ruby, "fib.resume == 3", fib);
    rb_assert!(ruby, "fib.resume == 5", fib);
    rb_assert!(ruby, "fib.resume == 8", fib);
    Ok(())
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/fiber.rs.html#148-191)#### pub fn [fiber_new_from_fn](https://docs.rs#method.fiber_new_from_fn)<F, R>(
    &self,
    storage: [Storage](https://docs.rs/fiber/enum.Storage.html),

#### pub fn [fiber_new_from_fn](https://docs.rs#method.fiber_new_from_fn)<F, R>(
    &self,
    storage: [Storage](https://docs.rs/fiber/enum.Storage.html),
    func: F,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Fiber](https://docs.rs/fiber/struct.Fiber.html), [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)>

**only.**

`ruby_gte_3_1`Create a Ruby Fiber.

See also [ fiber_new](https://docs.rs/struct.Ruby.html#method.fiber_new), which is more efficient when

`func` is a function or closure that does not capture any variables.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-85)Examples

```
use magnus::{rb_assert, Error, Ruby, Value};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut a = 0_u64;
    let mut b = 1_u64;
    let fib = ruby.fiber_new_from_fn(Default::default(), move |ruby, _args, _block| {
        while let Some(c) = a.checked_add(b) {
            let _: Value = ruby.fiber_yield((c,))?;
            a = b;
            b = c;
        }
        Ok(())
    })?;
    rb_assert!(ruby, "fib.resume == 1", fib);
    rb_assert!(ruby, "fib.resume == 2", fib);
    rb_assert!(ruby, "fib.resume == 3", fib);
    rb_assert!(ruby, "fib.resume == 5", fib);
    rb_assert!(ruby, "fib.resume == 8", fib);
    Ok(())
}
```

#### pub fn [fiber_yield](https://docs.rs#method.fiber_yield)<A, T>(&self, args: A) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)>

**only.**

`ruby_gte_3_1`Transfer execution back to where the current Fiber was resumed.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-87)Examples

```
use magnus::{rb_assert, value::Opaque, Error, Ruby, Value};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let ary = ruby.ary_new();
    let send_array = Opaque::from(ary);
    let fiber = ruby.fiber_new_from_fn(Default::default(), move |ruby, _args, _block| {
        let ary = ruby.get_inner(send_array);
        ary.push(1)?;
        let _: Value = ruby.fiber_yield(())?;
        ary.push(2)?;
        let _: Value = ruby.fiber_yield(())?;
        ary.push(3)?;
        let _: Value = ruby.fiber_yield(())?;
        Ok(())
    })?;
    ary.push("a")?;
    let _: Value = fiber.resume(())?;
    ary.push("b")?;
    let _: Value = fiber.resume(())?;
    ary.push("c")?;
    let _: Value = fiber.resume(())?;
    rb_assert!(ruby, r#"ary == ["a", 1, "b", 2, "c", 3]"#, ary);
    Ok(())
}

#### pub fn [gc_disable](https://docs.rs#method.gc_disable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Disable automatic GC runs.

This could result in other Ruby api functions unexpectedly raising
`NoMemError`.

Returns `true` if GC was already disabled, `false` otherwise.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-89)Examples

```
use magnus::{Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let was_disabled = ruby.gc_disable();
    // GC is off
    // return GC to previous state
    if !was_disabled {
        ruby.gc_enable();
    }
    Ok(())
}
```
Enable automatic GC run.

Garbage Collection is enabled by default, calling this function only
makes sense if [ disable](https://docs.rs/gc/fn.disable.html) was previously called.

Returns `true` if GC was previously disabled, `false` otherwise.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-90)Examples

```
use magnus::{Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let was_disabled = ruby.gc_enable();
    // GC is on
    // return GC to previous state
    if was_disabled {
        ruby.gc_disable();
    }
    Ok(())
}
```
Trigger a “full” GC run.

This will perform a full mark phase and a complete sweep phase, but may not run every single process associated with garbage collection.

Finalisers will be deferred to run later.

Currently (with versions of Ruby that support compaction) it will not trigger compaction.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-91)Examples

```
use magnus::{Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    ruby.gc_start();
    Ok(())
}

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/gc.rs.html#401-403)#### pub fn [gc_adjust_memory_usage](https://docs.rs#method.gc_adjust_memory_usage)(&self, diff: [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.isize.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/gc.rs.html#401-403)

#### pub fn [gc_adjust_memory_usage](https://docs.rs#method.gc_adjust_memory_usage)(&self, diff: [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.isize.html))

Inform Ruby of external memory usage.

The Ruby GC is run when Ruby thinks it’s running out of memory, but won’t take into account any memory allocated outside of Ruby api functions. This function can be used to give Ruby a more accurate idea of how much memory the process is using.

Pass negative numbers to indicate memory has been freed.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-92)Examples

```
use magnus::{Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let buf = Vec::<u8>::with_capacity(1024 * 1024);
    let mem_size = buf.capacity() * std::mem::size_of::<u8>();
    ruby.gc_adjust_memory_usage(mem_size as isize);
    // ...
    drop(buf);
    ruby.gc_adjust_memory_usage(-(mem_size as isize));
    Ok(())
}
```
Returns the number of garbage collections that have been run since the start of the process.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-93)Examples

```
use magnus::{Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let before = ruby.gc_count();
    ruby.gc_start();
    assert!(ruby.gc_count() > before);
    Ok(())
}

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/process.rs.html#58-73)#### pub fn [waitpid](https://docs.rs#method.waitpid)(
    &self,
    pid: [WaitTarget](https://docs.rs/process/enum.WaitTarget.html),
    flags: [Flags](https://docs.rs/process/struct.Flags.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<([NonZeroU32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/num/nonzero/type.NonZeroU32.html), [ExitStatus](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/process/struct.ExitStatus.html))>, [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/process.rs.html#58-73)

#### pub fn [waitpid](https://docs.rs#method.waitpid)(
    &self,
    pid: [WaitTarget](https://docs.rs/process/enum.WaitTarget.html),
    flags: [Flags](https://docs.rs/process/struct.Flags.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<([NonZeroU32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/num/nonzero/type.NonZeroU32.html), [ExitStatus](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/process/struct.ExitStatus.html))>, [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)>

Wait for a process.

This function releases Ruby’s Global VM Lock (GVL), so while it will block the current thread, other Ruby threads can be scheduled.

Returns the Process ID (PID) of the process waited, and its exit status.

If the `NOHANG` flag is passed this function will not block, instead it
will clean up an exited child process if there is one, or returns
`None` if there is no exited child process.

If the `UNTRACED` flag is passed, this function will also return
stopped processes (e.g. that can be resumed), not only exited processes.
For these stopped processes the exit status will be reported as
successful, although they have not yet exited.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-112)Examples

```
use std::process::Command;
use magnus::{process::WaitTarget, Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let child = Command::new("ls").spawn().unwrap();
    let (pid, status) = ruby
        .waitpid(WaitTarget::ChildPid(child.id()), Default::default())?
        .unwrap();
    assert_eq!(child.id(), pid.get());
    assert!(status.success());
    Ok(())
}
```

On creation this Array is hidden from Ruby, and must be consumed to pass it to Ruby (where it reverts to a regular untyped Array). It is then inaccessible to Rust.

```

    ary.push("1".parse().unwrap())?;
    ary.push("2.3".parse().unwrap())?;
    ary.push("4.5".parse().unwrap())?;
    rb_assert!(ruby, "ary == [1.0, 2.3, 4.5]", ary);
    // ary has moved and can no longer be used.
    Ok(())
}

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/r_struct.rs.html#426-431)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/r_struct.rs.html#426-431)

Define a Ruby Struct class.

`members` is a tuple of `&str`, of between lengths 1 to 12 inclusive.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-135)Examples

When providing `None` for the `name` the struct class’s name will be
taken from the first constant it is assigned to:

```
use magnus::{prelude::*, Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let struct_class = ruby.define_struct(None, ("foo", "bar"))?;
    ruby.define_global_const("Example", struct_class)?;
    assert_eq!(unsafe { struct_class.name().to_owned() }, "Example");
    let instance = struct_class.new_instance((1, 2))?;
    assert_eq!(instance.inspect(), "#<struct Example foo=1, bar=2>");
    Ok(())
}
```
When providing `Some("Name")` for the `name` the struct will be defined
under `Struct`:

```
use magnus::{prelude::*, Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let struct_class = ruby.define_struct(Some("Example"), ("foo", "bar"))?;
    assert_eq!(unsafe { struct_class.name().to_owned() }, "Struct::Example");
    let instance = struct_class.new_instance((1, 2))?;
    assert_eq!(instance.inspect(), "#<struct Struct::Example foo=1, bar=2>");
    Ok(())
}
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/r_struct.rs.html#458-463)

**only.**

`ruby_gte_3_3`Define a Ruby Data class.

If provided, `super_class` must be a subclass of Ruby’s `Data` class
(or `Data` itself).

`members` is a tuple of `&str`, of between lengths 1 to 12 inclusive.

```
use magnus::{kwargs, prelude::*, Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let data_class = ruby.define_data(None, ("foo", "bar"))?;
    ruby.define_global_const("Example", data_class)?;
    assert_eq!(unsafe { data_class.name().to_owned() }, "Example");
    let instance = data_class.new_instance((kwargs!("foo" => 1, "bar" => 2),))?;
    assert_eq!(instance.inspect(), "#<data Example foo=1, bar=2>");
    Ok(())
}

Allowing a wrapped type to be subclassed from Ruby:

(note, in this example `Point` does not have and does not call
the `initialize` method, subclasses would need to override the class
`new` method rather than `initialize`)

```
use magnus::{function, method, prelude::*, Error, RClass, RTypedData, Ruby, Value};
#[magnus::wrap(class = "Point")]
struct Point {
    x: isize,
    y: isize,
}
impl Point {
    fn new(ruby: &Ruby, class: RClass, x: isize, y: isize) -> RTypedData {
        ruby.wrap_as(Self { x, y }, class)
    }
}
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let point_class = ruby.define_class("Point", ruby.class_object())?;
    point_class.define_singleton_method("new", method!(Point::new, 2))?;
    point_class
        .define_singleton_method("inherited", function!(RClass::undef_default_alloc_func, 1))?;
    let value: Value = ruby.eval(
        r#"
          class SubPoint < Point
          end
          SubPoint.new(4, 2)
        "#,
    )?;
    assert!(value.is_kind_of(ruby.class_object().const_get::<_, RClass>("SubPoint")?));
    assert!(value.is_kind_of(point_class));
    Ok(())
}
```

#### pub fn [thread_schedule](https://docs.rs#method.thread_schedule)(&self)

Attempt to schedule another thread.

This function blocks until the current thread is re-scheduled.

Blocks until the given file descriptor is readable.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-145)Examples

```
use std::{
    io::{Read, Write},
    net::Shutdown,
    os::unix::net::UnixStream,
};
use magnus::{Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let (mut a, mut b) = UnixStream::pair().unwrap();
    a.write_all(b"hello, world!").unwrap();
    a.shutdown(Shutdown::Both).unwrap();
    b.set_nonblocking(true).unwrap();
    ruby.thread_wait_fd(&b)?;
    let mut s = String::new();
    b.read_to_string(&mut s).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(s, "hello, world!");
    Ok(())
}
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/thread.rs.html#395-401)#### pub fn [thread_check_ints](https://docs.rs#method.thread_check_ints)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/thread.rs.html#395-401)

#### pub fn [thread_check_ints](https://docs.rs#method.thread_check_ints)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)>

Check for, and run, pending interrupts.

While Ruby is running a native extension function (such as one written
in Rust with Magnus) it can’t process interrupts (e.g. signals or
`Thread#raise` called from another thread). Periodically calling this
function in any long running function will check for *and run* any
queued interrupts. This will allow your long running function to be
interrupted with say ctrl-c or `Timeout::timeout`.

If any interrupt raises an error it will be returned as `Err`.

Calling this function may execute code on another thread.

Create a new `Time` in the local timezone.

    rb_assert!(ruby, r#"t == Time.new(2022, 5, 31, 9, 8, 0, "-07:00")"#, t);
    Ok(())
}

#### pub fn [get_inner](https://docs.rs#method.get_inner)<T>(&self, wrapper: impl [InnerValue](https://docs.rs/value/trait.InnerValue.html)<Value = T>) -> T

Get the inner value from `wrapper`.

`self` acts as a token proving this is called from a Ruby thread and
thus it is safe to return the inner value. See [ Opaque](https://docs.rs/value/struct.Opaque.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/value/struct.Lazy.html)

`Lazy`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-155)Examples

```
use magnus::{rb_assert, value::Opaque, Ruby};
let ruby = Ruby::get().unwrap();
let opaque_str = Opaque::from(ruby.str_new("example"));
// send to another Ruby thread
let ruby = Ruby::get().unwrap(); // errors on non-Ruby thread
let str = ruby.get_inner(opaque_str);
rb_assert!(ruby, r#"str == "example""#, str);
```
```
use magnus::{rb_assert, value::Lazy, RString, Ruby};
static STATIC_STR: Lazy<RString> = Lazy::new(|ruby| ruby.str_new("example"));
let ruby = Ruby::get().unwrap(); // errors if Ruby not initialised
let str = ruby.get_inner(&STATIC_STR);
rb_assert!(ruby, r#"str == "example""#, str);

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/lib.rs.html#2372-2390)#### pub fn [call_super](https://docs.rs#method.call_super)<A, T>(&self, args: A) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/lib.rs.html#2372-2390)

#### pub fn [call_super](https://docs.rs#method.call_super)<A, T>(&self, args: A) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)>

Call the super method of the current method context.

Returns `Ok(T)` if the super method exists and returns without error,
and the return value converts to a `T`, or returns `Err` if there is no
super method, the super method raises or the conversion fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-174)Examples

```
use magnus::{function, prelude::*, rb_assert, Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let a = ruby.eval(
        r#"
          class A
            def test
              "Hello from A"
            end
          end
          A
        "#,
    )?;
    let b = ruby.define_class("B", a)?;
    fn test(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<String, Error> {
        let s: String = ruby.call_super(())?;
        Ok(format!("{}, and hello from B", s))
    }
    b.define_method("test", function!(test, 0))?;
    rb_assert!(ruby, r#"B.new.test == "Hello from A, and hello from B""#);
    Ok(())
}
```
Evaluate a string of Ruby code, converting the result to a `T`.

Ruby will use the ‘ASCII-8BIT’ (aka binary) encoding for any Ruby
string literals in the passed string of Ruby code. See the
[ eval](https://docs.rs/macro.eval.html) macro for an alternative that supports
utf-8.

Errors if `s` contains a null byte, the conversion fails, or on an
uncaught Ruby exception.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-176)Examples

```
use magnus::{Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    assert_eq!(ruby.eval::<i64>("1 + 2")?, 3);
    Ok(())
}
```

# setup in magnus::embed - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/embed/fn.setup.html

`pub unsafe fn setup() -> `[Cleanup](https://docs.rs/struct.Cleanup.html)**crate feature**only.

`embed`## Expand description

Performs basic initialisation of the Ruby VM.

This only initialises the core of Ruby’s functionality, some features may
be missing or not work as expected. Generally [ init](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html) should be preferred,
but there may be some cases where it is not possible to run the full Ruby
initialisation sequence.

Calling this function is only required when embedding Ruby in Rust. It is not required when embedding Rust in Ruby, e.g. in a Ruby Gem.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Must be called in `main()`, or at least a function higher up the stack than
any code calling Ruby. Must not drop Cleanup until the very end of the
process, after all Ruby execution has finished. Do not use Ruby values
after Cleanup has been dropped.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if this, [ init](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html), or

[are collectively called more than once.](https://docs.rs/struct.Ruby.html#method.init)

`Ruby::init`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
let ruby = unsafe { magnus::embed::setup() };
let result: i64 = ruby.eval("2 + 2").unwrap();
assert_eq!(result, 4);
```

# DataTypeFunctions in magnus::typed_data - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/typed_data/trait.DataTypeFunctions.html

pub trait DataTypeFunctions{
    // Provided methods
    fn
```
[free](https://docs.rs#method.free)(self: [Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<Self>) { ... }

}## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Called when the Ruby wrapper object is garbage collected.

This can be implemented to perform Ruby-specific clean up when your
type is no longer referenced from Ruby, but it is likely easier to do
this in a [ Drop](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html) implementation for your type.

This function will always be called by Ruby on GC, it can not be opted out of.

The default implementation simply drops `self`.

If this function (or the [ Drop](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html) implementation for your type) call
Ruby APIs you should not enable the

`free_immediately` flag with the
[/](https://docs.rs/attr.wrap.html)

`wrap`[macro or](https://docs.rs/derive.TypedData.html)

`TypedData`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.DataTypeBuilder.html#method.free_immediately)

`DataTypeBuilder::free_immediately`This function **must not** panic. The process will abort if this
function panics.

Called when Ruby marks this object as part of garbage collection.

If your type contains any Ruby values you must mark each of those values in this function to avoid them being garbage collected.

This function is only called when the `mark` flag is set with the
[ wrap](https://docs.rs/attr.wrap.html)/

[macro or](https://docs.rs/derive.TypedData.html)

`TypedData`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.DataTypeBuilder.html#method.mark)

`DataTypeBuilder::mark`The default implementation does nothing.

This function **must not** panic. The process will abort if this
function panics.

Called by Ruby to establish the memory size of this data, to optimise when garbage collection happens.

This function is only called when the `size` flag is set with the
[ wrap](https://docs.rs/attr.wrap.html)/

[macro or](https://docs.rs/derive.TypedData.html)

`TypedData`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.DataTypeBuilder.html#method.mark)

`DataTypeBuilder::mark`The default implementation delegates to [ std::mem::size_of_val](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/mem/fn.size_of_val.html).

This function **must not** panic. The process will abort if this
function panics.

Called during garbage collection.

If your type contains any Ruby values that you have marked as moveable
in your [ mark](https://docs.rs/trait.DataTypeFunctions.html#method.mark) function, you must update them in this
function using

[.](https://docs.rs/gc/struct.Compactor.html#method.location)

`gc::Compactor::location`Ruby considers values are moveable if marked with the
[ gc::Marker::mark_movable](https://docs.rs/gc/struct.Marker.html#method.mark_movable) function. Other marking functions such as

[will prevent values being moved.](https://docs.rs/gc/struct.Marker.html#method.mark)

`gc::Marker::mark`As it is only safe for this function to receive a shared `&self`
reference, you must implement interior mutability to be able to update
values. This is very hard to do correctly, and it is recommended to
simply avoid using [ gc::Marker::mark_movable](https://docs.rs/gc/struct.Marker.html#method.mark_movable) and

`compact`.This function is only called when the `compact` flag is set with the
[ wrap](https://docs.rs/attr.wrap.html)/

[macro or](https://docs.rs/derive.TypedData.html)

`TypedData`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.DataTypeBuilder.html#method.mark)

`DataTypeBuilder::mark`The default implementation does nothing.

This function **must not** panic. The process will abort if this
function panics.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# magnus::encoding - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/encoding/index.html

## Expand description

Types and functions for working with encodings.

This module defines 3 types for working with encodings, these types can
be converted back and forth with [ From](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)/

[like so:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)

`Into````
Encoding <-> RbEncoding <-> Index
      |______________________^
```
Many functions that require an encoding take their arguments as
`Into<RbEncoding>` or `Into<Index>` to ease working with the different
types. The type specified for the `Into` conversion hints at the type the
function natively works with, and thus will avoid any conversion cost.

[ Encoding](https://docs.rs/struct.Encoding.html) and

[both implement](https://docs.rs/struct.RbEncoding.html)

`RbEncoding`[and](https://docs.rs/try_convert/trait.TryConvert.html)

`TryConvert`[so can be used as parameters and return values in functions bound to Ruby. Both convert from either an instance of](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoValue.html)

`IntoValue``Encoding` or a
string of an encoding name, and convert to an instance of `Encoding`.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Encoding](https://docs.rs/struct.Encoding.html)
- Wrapper type for a Value known to be an instance of Ruby’s Encoding class.
- [Index](https://docs.rs/struct.Index.html)
- The index of an encoding in Ruby’s internal encodings table.
- [RbEncoding](https://docs.rs/struct.RbEncoding.html)
- Ruby’s internal encoding type.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [CType](https://docs.rs/enum.CType.html)
- A character type.
- [Coderange](https://docs.rs/enum.Coderange.html)
- Possible states of how a string matches its encoding.
- [MbcLen](https://docs.rs/enum.MbcLen.html)
- Return value for `RbEncoding::precise_mbclen`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Encoding](https://docs.rs/trait.EncodingCapable.html)- Capable
- Trait that marks Ruby types cable of having an encoding.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [check](https://docs.rs/fn.check.html)
- Returns the common encoding between `v1`and`v2`, or`Err`.
- [compatible](https://docs.rs/fn.compatible.html)
- Returns the common encoding between `v1`and`v2`, or`None`.
- [copy](https://docs.rs/fn.copy.html)
- Compies the encoding from `src`to`dst`.

# magnus::rb_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/rb_sys/index.html

**crate feature**only.

`rb-sys`## Expand description

Functions for interoperability with rb-sys.

These functions are provided to interface with the lower-level Ruby
bindings provided by [rb-sys](https://docs.rs/rb-sys/0.9.128/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rb_sys/index.html). You may want to use rb-sys when:

- Magnus does not provide access to a Ruby API because the API can not be made safe & ergonomic.
- Magnus exposed the API in a way that does not work for your use case.
- The API just hasn’t been implemented yet.

Even if you are not in a position to contribute code to Magnus, please
[open an issue](https://github.com/matsadler/magnus/issues) outlining your
use case and the APIs you need whenever you find yourself reaching for this
module.

[§](https://docs.rs#stability)Stability

Functions in this module are considered unstable. While there is no plan to alter or remove them, non-backwards compatible changes in this module will not necessarily be considered as SemVer major changes.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

The unsafe functions in this module are capable of producing values that break the safety guarantees of almost every other function in Magnus. Use them with care.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [AsRawId](https://docs.rs/trait.AsRawId.html)
- Trait to convert a `Id``ID`
- [AsRaw](https://docs.rs/trait.AsRawValue.html)- Value
- Converts from a `Value``VALUE`
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRawId.html)- RawId
- Trait to convert from a raw `ID``Id`
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRawValue.html)- RawValue
- Converts from a raw `VALUE``Value`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [catch_](https://docs.rs/fn.catch_unwind.html)- unwind
- Attempts to catch cases of Rust unwinding, converting to a fatal `Error`
- [protect](https://docs.rs/fn.protect.html)
- Calls the given closure, catching all cases of unwinding from Ruby
returning them as an `Error`
- [resume_](https://docs.rs/fn.resume_error.html)- error - ⚠
- Resumes an `Error``protect`

# magnus::scan_args - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/scan_args/index.html

## Expand description

Types and functions for complex method arguments.

Ruby’s APIs to define methods, exposed in magnus through functions such as
[ define_method](https://docs.rs/module/trait.Module.html#method.define_method) and the

[macro, allow defining methods with a fixed number of positional arguments, or an unbounded collection of arguments as a slice or Ruby array. The functions in this module allow for more complex argument handling.](https://docs.rs/macro.method.html)

`method`Ruby arguments can be classified as follows:

```
def example(a, b, c=nil, d=nil, *rest, e, f, g:, h:, i: nil, j: nil, **kwargs, &block)
            \__/  \__________/  \___/  \__/  \____/  \____________/  \______/  \____/
              |        |          |      |     |            |           |        |
           required    |        splat    |  keywords     keywords    keywords  block
                    optional             | (required)   (optional)   (splat)
                                         |
                                      trailing
                                      required
```
The [ scan_args](https://docs.rs/fn.scan_args.html) function can be used with a method defined as

`method!(name, -1)` (i.e. receiving a slice of arguments) to implement this
more complex functionality.The [ get_kwargs](https://docs.rs/fn.get_kwargs.html) function is used to extract keywords from a Ruby

`Hash`
of keywords and implement the behaviour around required and optional
keyword arguments.See also [ Ruby](https://docs.rs/struct.Ruby.html#argument-parsing).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Args](https://docs.rs/struct.Args.html)
- Arguments returned from `scan_args`
- [KwArgs](https://docs.rs/struct.KwArgs.html)
- Arguments returned from `get_kwargs`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Scan](https://docs.rs/trait.ScanArgsBlock.html)- Args - Block
- Trait implemented for types that can be retrieved as a block argument by
`scan_args`
- [Scan](https://docs.rs/trait.ScanArgsKw.html)- Args - Kw
- Trait implemented for types that can be retrieved as keyword arguments by
`scan_args`
- [Scan](https://docs.rs/trait.ScanArgsOpt.html)- Args - Opt
- Trait implemented for types that can be retrieved as optional arguments by
`scan_args`
- [Scan](https://docs.rs/trait.ScanArgsRequired.html)- Args - Required
- Trait implemented for types that can be retrieved as required arguments by
`scan_args`
- [Scan](https://docs.rs/trait.ScanArgsSplat.html)- Args - Splat
- Trait implemented for types that can be retrieved a ‘splat’ argument by
`scan_args`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_arity.html)- arity - `old-api`
- Returns `Err`containing a Ruby`ArgumentError`if`len`is not within`bounds`.
- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_kwargs.html)- kwargs
- Deconstruct keyword arguments.
- [scan_](https://docs.rs/fn.scan_args.html)- args
- Retrieves arguments from a slice.

# data_type_builder in magnus - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/macro.data_type_builder.html

```
macro_rules! data_type_builder {
    ($t:ty, $name:literal) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Create a new [ DataTypeBuilder](https://docs.rs/typed_data/struct.DataTypeBuilder.html).

`name` should be unique per wrapped type. It does not need to be a
valid Ruby identifier.

`data_type_builder!(Example, "example")` is equivalent to
`DataTypeBuilder::<Example>::new` with a `name` argument of `"example"` as
a `'static CStr`.

Create a new `DataTypeBuilder`.

`name` should be unique per wrapped type. It does not need to be a
valid Ruby identifier.

See [ data_type_builder](https://docs.rs/macro.data_type_builder.html) to create a

`DataTypeBuilder` with a `'static CStr` `name` from a string literal.Enable using the the `mark` function from `<T as DataTypeFunctions>`.

Enable using the the `compact` function from `<T as DataTypeFunctions>`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/typed_data.rs.html#296-299)#### pub const fn [free_immediately](https://docs.rs#method.free_immediately)(self) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/typed_data.rs.html#296-299)

#### pub const fn [free_immediately](https://docs.rs#method.free_immediately)(self) -> Self

Enable the ‘free_immediately’ flag.

This is safe to do as long as the `<T as DataTypeFunctions>::free`
function or `T`’s drop function don’t call Ruby in any way.

If safe this should be enabled as this performs better and is more memory efficient.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/typed_data.rs.html#311-314)#### pub const fn [wb_protected](https://docs.rs#method.wb_protected)(self) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/typed_data.rs.html#311-314)

#### pub const fn [wb_protected](https://docs.rs#method.wb_protected)(self) -> Self

Enable the ‘write barrier protected’ flag.

Types that contain Ruby values by default do not participate in
generational GC (they are scanned every GC). This flag asserts all
operations that write Ruby values to this type are protected with
write barriers (see [ Writebarrier::writebarrier](https://docs.rs/trait.Writebarrier.html#method.writebarrier)) so this
type can participate in generational GC.

The write barrier is hard to get right. Magnus recommends you do not use this flag.

## Expand description

Wrap a Rust function item with Ruby type conversion and error handling,
ignoring Ruby’s `self` argument.

This macro wraps the given function and returns a function pointer
implementing the [ Method](https://docs.rs/method/trait.Method.html) trait, suitable for passing to functions that
define Ruby methods such as

[.](https://docs.rs/module/trait.Module.html#method.define_method)

`define_method`Ruby code implicitly always has a `self` parameter available. In the
extension API this is passed explicitly. The wrapper this macro generates
ignores that argument, and does not pass it to the wrapped function.

The values `-2` and `-1` for `arity` have special meaning. Both indicate
functions with any number of arguments, with `-2` the arguments are passed
as a [ RArray](https://docs.rs/r_array/struct.RArray.html), with

`-1` they are passed as a slice of [s. Arity of](https://docs.rs/value/struct.Value.html)

`Value``-1` can be used with [and](https://docs.rs/scan_args/fn.scan_args.html)

`scan_args`[for more complex method signatures.](https://docs.rs/scan_args/fn.get_kwargs.html)

`get_kwargs`| Arity | Signature |
|---|---|
| -2 | `fn(arguments: RArray) -> Result<R, Error>` |
| -1 | `fn(arguments: &[Value]) -> Result<R, Error>` |
| 0 | `fn()-> Result<R, Error>` |
| 1 | `fn(arg1: T) -> Result<R, Error>` |
| 2 | `fn(arg1: T, arg2: U) -> Result<R, Error>` |
| … | … |
| 16 | … |

Where `T`, `U`, and so on are any types that implement `TryConvert`,
and `R` implements [ IntoValue](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoValue.html). It is also possible to return just

`R`
rather than a `Result` for functions that will never error, and omit the
return value (i.e. return `()`) for a function that returns `nil` to Ruby.
See [for more details on what can be returned.](https://docs.rs/method/trait.ReturnValue.html)

`ReturnValue`See the [ method](https://docs.rs/macro.method.html) macro for cases where the

`self`
argument is required.[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
fn distance(a: (f64, f64), b: (f64, f64)) -> f64 {
    ((b.0 - a.0).powi(2) + (b.0 - a.0).powi(2)).sqrt()
}
#[magnus::init]
fn init(ruby: &magnus::Ruby) {
    ruby.define_global_function("distance", magnus::function!(distance, 2));
}
```

# rb_assert in magnus - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/macro.rb_assert.html

```
macro_rules! rb_assert {
    ($expr:literal) => { ... };
    ($expr:literal, $($bindings:tt)*) => { ... };
    ($ruby:expr, $expr:literal) => { ... };
    ($ruby:expr, $expr:literal, $($bindings:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Asserts a Ruby expression evaluates to a truthy value.

This macro uses the Ruby
[ power_assert](https://github.com/ruby/power_assert) gem that is part of
the Ruby standard library to generate detailed failure messages.

Outputs:

```
thread 'main' panicked at '
1 + 2 == 4
  |   |
  |   false
  3', src/lib.rs:5:1
```
[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if called from a non-Ruby thread.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

`magnus::rb_assert!("1 + 2 == 3");`Passing [ Ruby](https://docs.rs/struct.Ruby.html) to avoid the Ruby thread check:

```
let ruby = magnus::Ruby::get().unwrap();
magnus::rb_assert!(ruby, "1 + 2 == 3");
```
Making local variables accessible to Ruby:

```
let a = 1;
let b = 2;
magnus::rb_assert!("a + b == 3", a, b);
```
Directly setting local variables:

`magnus::rb_assert!("a + b == 3", a = 1, b = 2);`

# Enumerator in magnus - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/struct.Enumerator.html

`pub struct Enumerator(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

Wrapper type for a Value known to be an instance of Ruby’s Enumerator class.

`Enumerator` implements [ Iterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html), however Rust’s iterators are a pull
based model, whereas Ruby’s enumerators are a push based model. Bridging
these two models incurs a performance penalty, so

`Enumerator` may not be
the most performant way of iterating a collection.See the [ ReprValue](https://docs.rs/value/trait.ReprValue.html) and

[traits for additional methods available on this type.](https://docs.rs/trait.Object.html)

`Object`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use magnus::{prelude::*, rb_assert, Error, Ruby};
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let s = ruby.str_new("foo\nbar\nbaz");
    let results = ruby.ary_new();
    // `enumeratorize` returns `Enumerator`
    for line in s.enumeratorize("each_line", ()) {
        results.push(line?)?;
    }
    rb_assert!(r#"results == ["foo\n", "bar\n", "baz"]"#, results);
    Ok(())
}
```

# RTypedData in magnus - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/struct.RTypedData.html

`pub struct RTypedData(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

A Value pointer to a RTypedData struct, Ruby’s internal representation of objects that wrap foreign types.

See also [ typed_data::Obj](https://docs.rs/typed_data/struct.Obj.html).

See the [ ReprValue](https://docs.rs/value/trait.ReprValue.html) and

[traits for additional methods available on this type. See](https://docs.rs/trait.Object.html)

`Object`[for methods to create an](https://docs.rs/struct.Ruby.html#rtypeddata)

`Ruby``RTypedData`.## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/r_typed_data.rs.html#172-408)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-RTypedData)### impl [RTypedData](https://docs.rs/struct.RTypedData.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/r_typed_data.rs.html#172-408)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-RTypedData)

### impl [RTypedData](https://docs.rs/struct.RTypedData.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/r_typed_data.rs.html#199-204)#### pub fn [from_value](https://docs.rs#method.from_value)(val: [Value](https://docs.rs/value/struct.Value.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/magnus/r_typed_data.rs.html#199-204)

#### pub fn [from_value](https://docs.rs#method.from_value)(val: [Value](https://docs.rs/value/struct.Value.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self>

Return `Some(RTypedData)` if `val` is a `RTypedData`, `None` otherwise.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use magnus::{function, prelude::*, Error, RTypedData, Ruby};
#[magnus::wrap(class = "Point")]
struct Point {
    x: isize,
    y: isize,
}
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let point_class = ruby.define_class("Point", ruby.class_object())?;
    point_class.define_singleton_method("new", function!(|x, y| Point { x, y }, 2))?;
    assert!(RTypedData::from_value(ruby.eval(r#"Point.new(1, 2)"#)?).is_some());
    assert!(RTypedData::from_value(ruby.eval(r#"Object.new"#)?).is_none());
    Ok(())
}
```
Wrap the Rust type `T` in a Ruby object.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if called from a non-Ruby thread. See [ Ruby::wrap](https://docs.rs/struct.Ruby.html#method.wrap) for the
non-panicking version.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use magnus::{class, define_class, prelude::*, RTypedData};
#[magnus::wrap(class = "Point")]
struct Point {
    x: isize,
    y: isize,
}
let point_class = define_class("Point", class::object()).unwrap();
let value = RTypedData::wrap(Point { x: 4, y: 2 });
assert!(value.is_kind_of(point_class));
```
Wrap the Rust type `T` in a Ruby object that is an instance of the
given `class`.

See also [ TypedData::class_for](https://docs.rs/typed_data/trait.TypedData.html#method.class_for).

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-1)Panics

Panics if `class` is not a subclass of `<T as TypedData>::class()`, or
if called from a non-Ruby thread. See [ Ruby::wrap_as](https://docs.rs/struct.Ruby.html#method.wrap_as) for a version
that can not be called from a non-Ruby thread, so will not panic for
that reason.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use magnus::{class, define_class, prelude::*, RTypedData};
#[magnus::wrap(class = "Point")]
struct Point {
    x: isize,
    y: isize,
}
let point_class = define_class("Point", class::object()).unwrap();
let point_sub_class = define_class("SubPoint", point_class).unwrap();
let value = RTypedData::wrap_as(Point { x: 4, y: 2 }, point_sub_class);
assert!(value.is_kind_of(point_sub_class));
assert!(value.is_kind_of(point_class));
```
Allowing a wrapped type to be subclassed from Ruby:

(note, in this example `Point` does not have and does not call
the `initialize` method, subclasses would need to override the class
`new` method rather than `initialize`)

```
use magnus::{
    class, define_class, eval, function, method, prelude::*, RClass, RTypedData, Value,
};
#[magnus::wrap(class = "Point")]
struct Point {
    x: isize,
    y: isize,
}
impl Point {
    fn new(class: RClass, x: isize, y: isize) -> RTypedData {
        RTypedData::wrap_as(Self { x, y }, class)
    }
}
let point_class = define_class("Point", class::object()).unwrap();
point_class
    .define_singleton_method("new", method!(Point::new, 2))
    .unwrap();
point_class
    .define_singleton_method("inherited", function!(RClass::undef_default_alloc_func, 1))
    .unwrap();
let value: Value = eval(
    r#"
      class SubPoint < Point
      end
      SubPoint.new(4, 2)
    "#,
)
.unwrap();
assert!(value.is_kind_of(class::object().const_get::<_, RClass>("SubPoint").unwrap()));
assert!(value.is_kind_of(point_class));
```
Get a reference to the Rust type wrapped in the Ruby object `self`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
use magnus::{Error, Ruby};
#[magnus::wrap(class = "Point")]
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Point {
    x: isize,
    y: isize,
}
fn example(ruby: &Ruby) -> Result<(), Error> {
    ruby.define_class("Point", ruby.class_object())?;
    let value = ruby.wrap(Point { x: 4, y: 2 });
    assert_eq!(value.get::<Point>()?, &Point { x: 4, y: 2 });
    Ok(())
}
```

# IntoValueFromNative in magnus - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/trait.IntoValueFromNative.html

`pub unsafe trait IntoValueFromNative: `[IntoValue](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoValue.html) { }## Expand description

Conversions from Rust types that do not contain [ Value](https://docs.rs/value/struct.Value.html) into

[.](https://docs.rs/value/struct.Value.html)

`Value`This trait is used as a bound in functions such as
[ RArray::from_vec](https://docs.rs/r_array/struct.RArray.html#method.from_vec) to prevent accepting
heap allocated datastructures containing

`Value`, as it is not safe to
store a `Value` on the heap.[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

This trait must not be implemented for types that contain `Value`.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

## Implementations on Foreign Types[§](https://docs.rs#foreign-impls)

# call_super in magnus - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/fn.call_super.html

**crate feature**only.

`old-api`## Expand description

Call the super method of the current method context.

Returns `Ok(T)` if the super method exists and returns without error, and
the return value converts to a `T`, or returns `Err` if there is no super
method, the super method raises or the conversion fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if called from a non-Ruby thread. See [ Ruby::call_super](https://docs.rs/struct.Ruby.html#method.call_super) for the
non-panicking version.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use magnus::{call_super, define_class, eval, function, prelude::*, rb_assert, Error};
let a = eval(
    r#"
      class A
        def example
          "Hello from A"
        end
      end
      A
    "#,
)
.unwrap();
let b = define_class("B", a).unwrap();
fn example() -> Result<String, Error> {
    let s: String = call_super(())?;
    Ok(format!("{}, and hello from B", s))
}
b.define_method("example", function!(example, 0)).unwrap();
rb_assert!(r#"B.new.example == "Hello from A, and hello from B""#)
```

---

# current_receiver in magnus - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/fn.current_receiver.html

Available on

**crate feature**only.`old-api`## Expand description

Return the Ruby `self` of the current method context.

Returns `Err` if called outside a method context or the conversion fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if called from a non-Ruby thread. See [ Ruby::current_receiver](https://docs.rs/struct.Ruby.html#method.current_receiver) for
the non-panicking version.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use magnus::{
    current_receiver, define_global_function, method, prelude::*, rb_assert, Error, Value,
};
fn example(rb_self: Value) -> Result<bool, Error> {
    rb_self.equal(current_receiver::<Value>()?)
}
define_global_function("example", method!(example, 0));
rb_assert!("example");
```

# define_class in magnus - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/fn.define_class.html

Available on

**crate feature**only.`old-api`## Expand description

Define a class in the root scope.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if called from a non-Ruby thread. See [ Ruby::define_class](https://docs.rs/struct.Ruby.html#method.define_class) for the
non-panicking version.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use magnus::{class, define_class, rb_assert};
define_class("Example", class::object()).unwrap();
rb_assert!("Example.is_a?(Class)");
```

# define_global_function in magnus - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/fn.define_global_function.html

`pub fn define_global_function<M>(name: &`[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html), func: M)Available on

**crate feature**only.`old-api`## Expand description

Define a method in the root scope.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if called from a non-Ruby thread. See
[ Ruby::define_global_function](https://docs.rs/struct.Ruby.html#method.define_global_function) for the non-panicking version.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use magnus::{define_global_function, function, rb_assert};

    format!("Hello, {}!", subject)

define_global_function("greet", function!(greet, 1));
rb_assert!(r#"greet("world") == "Hello, world!""#);
```

# define_variable in magnus - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/fn.define_variable.html

Available on

**crate feature**only.`old-api`## Expand description

Define a global variable.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if called from a non-Ruby thread. See [ Ruby::define_variable](https://docs.rs/struct.Ruby.html#method.define_variable) for
the non-panicking version.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use magnus::{define_variable, prelude::*, rb_assert, RString};
let v = define_variable("example", 42).unwrap();
rb_assert!("$example == 42");
// safe as long as another thread isn't modifying v
unsafe {
    *v = RString::new("answer").as_value();
}
rb_assert!(r#"$example == "answer""#);
```

# DataTypeFunctions in magnus - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/magnus/0.8.2/magnus/derive.DataTypeFunctions.html

Derives DataTypeFunctions with default implementations, for simple uses
of TypedData.

For cases where no custom DataTypeFunctions are required a default
implementation can be derived. The wrap macro may be a simpler
alternative in this use case.
